# 21 Famous Authors and Their Pen Names

[![Image 8](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/34af0ec9a3dc985545a5561089fed4cda74817566b98f97814033e50217ed4ce?s=24&d=identicon&r=g)](https://blog.enotes.com/author/savcotten/ "Posts by  ")[Savannah Cotten](https://blog.enotes.com/author/savcotten/)February 2, 20180 Comments

For centuries, writers have created pen names to publish their literary works. Adopting a pseudonym grants writers the ability to conceal their true identity for personal, political, and ethical reasons. Some of our literary world’s most beloved, bestselling authors have formulated their entire careers using alternative identities. Female writers, especially [during the 19th century](https://www.enotes.com/topics/feminism/critical-essays/women-19th-century), have often used male pen names to combat sexism and prejudice in a traditionally male-dominated craft.

Other reasons for using a _nom de plume_ include privacy, avoiding overexposure, crossing into different genres, creating a sense of individuality, and even simplifying one’s birth name in hopes of making it more memorable. Whatever the case may be, choosing a pen name remains a personal choice that ultimately aids writers in their publishing pursuits.

Here’s a list of 21 famous writers and their real names you might not have known until now!

![Image 9: Copy of Authors](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/copy-of-authors.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)

### 1. [Anne Rice](https://www.enotes.com/topics/anne-rice)

**Real Name: Howard Allen Frances O’Brien**

Originally named after her father, the author of _[Vampire Chronicles](https://www.enotes.com/topics/vampire-chronicles)_ changed her name to “Anne” upon her first day of school to avoid being bullied. After marrying her now deceased husband Stan Rice, she used her married name to publish the majority of her work. Rice adopted a couple other pen names including Anne Rampling and A.N Roquelaure when she [published some erotic novels](http://newsfeed.time.com/2013/07/15/famous-authors-with-secret-pseudonyms/slide/anne-rice-anne-rampling-a-n-roquelaure/).

### ![Image 10: 17](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/17-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)2. [Dr. Seuss](https://www.enotes.com/topics/theodor-seuss-geisel)

**Real Name: Theodor Seuss Geisel**

Dr. Seuss, one of the more well-known pen names, was adopted from Geisel’s middle name once he started writing children’s books. He added the “Dr.” because [his father had always wanted him to pursue a career in medicine](http://www.adweek.com/galleycat/authors-and-their-pseudonyms-infographic/119763). Some say that Geisel was [saving his real name to one day publish his “great American novel”;](http://m.seussville.com/biography.html)others suggest that Geisel simply felt more inclined to tell an “entertaining” story rather than a “true” one.

### ![Image 11: 18](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/18-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)3. [Mark Twain](https://www.enotes.com/topics/mark-twain)

**Real Name: Samuel Clemens**

While scholars have never been clear about the origin of Clemens’s pseudonym, the most [recent investigations suggest](https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2013/10/now-we-know-how-samuel-clemens-became-mark-twain/310292/) that the name Mark Twain came from a short-lived, popular humor journal that he often read. Other stories indicate that Mark Twain had been used by Clemens’s former riverboat captain when he worked on the Mississippi river. [If the man checking the depth called out “mark twain,” it meant a depth of twelve feet](https://www.marktwainmuseum.org/frequently-asked-questions/)—meaning that the water was safe for riverboats that day.

### ![Image 12: 19](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/19-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)4. Currer, Ellis, & Acton Bell

**Real Names: [Charlotte, Emily, & Anne Brontë](https://www.enotes.com/topics/brontes)**

In 19th-century England, [women were not permitted to publish poetry](https://www.enotes.com/topics/feminism/critical-essays/womens-literature-19th-century), so the Brontë sisters created the pen names of Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell. Each male pseudonym matched the corresponding sisters’ names, helping them publish their first anthology of poetry in 1846. Initially, Emily’s [_Wuthering Heights_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/wuthering-heights) and Charlotte’s [_Jane Eyre_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/jane-eyre) were both published under their male names. It wasn’t until the Brontë sisters traveled to London to meet their publisher in person were their true identities revealed and, fortunately, they were given the credit they deserved.

### ![Image 13: 20](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/20-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)5. Boz

**Real Name: [Charles Dickens](https://www.enotes.com/topics/charles-dickens)**

In the early stages of Dickens’s writing career, the author often published his work anonymously. It was not until one of Dickens’s earliest pieces of fiction titled “The Boarding House” featured an epithet that was signed by “The Inimitable Boz.” Boz was originally derived from the nickname Dickens had given his younger brother, Augustus. [Dickens would call him “Moses” after a character in Oliver Goldsmith’s _The Vicar of Wakefield_](https://blog.bookstellyouwhy.com/bid/317643/Famous-Authors-and-Their-Pseudonyms-Part-One). Pronounced through the nose, the name became Boses, and was easily shortened to Boz.

### ![Image 14: 21](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/21-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)6. A.M. Barnard

**Real Name: [Louisa May Alcott](https://www.enotes.com/topics/louisa-may-alcott)**

Early in her writing career, Alcott used the pen name Flora Fairfield to publish her poems and short stories throughout the 1850s. A decade later, some of Alcott’s melodramas were produced in Boston theatre under the pseudonym, A.M. Barnard. Knowledge of Alcott’s alias did not surface until the 1970s when [historians discovered letters from the author](http://newsfeed.time.com/2013/07/15/famous-authors-with-secret-pseudonyms/slide/louisa-may-alcott-a-m-barnard/) signing off with the androgynous pseudonym. Digging deeper, they were able to find other works published by Barnard in various periodicals.

### ![Image 15: 22](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/22-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)7. [C.S. Lewis](https://www.enotes.com/topics/cs-lewis)

**Real Name: Clive Staple Lewis**

Lewis published his first work titled [_Spirits in Bondage_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/c-s-lewis-62010/critical-essays/principal-works) (1919) under the name, Clive Hamilton to [avoid ruining his reputation as a tutor at Oxford University](https://www.stylist.co.uk/books/15-authors-who-used-pseudonyms/126657). The name was adapted from the author’s birth name and his mother’s maiden name. After Lewis’s wife passed away in 1960, he went on to publish a few more works under the name N.W. Clerk to again avoid being identified as the author. Eventually, Lewis published some of his [greatest literary works](https://www.enotes.com/authors/lewis-carroll) under his abbreviated birth name.

### ![Image 16: 23](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/23-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)8. Silence Dogood

**Real Name: [Benjamin Franklin](https://www.enotes.com/topics/benjamin-franklin)**

Franklin created several pseudonyms during his lifetime, each one possessing an ironically witty persona. His first pen name was [Silence Dogood](http://www.pbs.org/benfranklin/l3_wit_name.html), a satirical middle-aged widower whom Franklin created when he was only fifteen years old. Some of his other pen names include Caelia Shortface, Martha Careful, Richard Saunders ([_Poor Richard’s Almanack_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/poor-richards-almanack)), Busy Body, Anthony Afterwit, Polly Baker, and Benevolus. Franklin is one of the few male writers to take on a female alias—in fact, he often used his feminine personas to create a social critique of the patriarchy.

### ![Image 17: 24](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/24-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)9. [George Eliot](https://www.enotes.com/topics/george-eliot)

**Real Name: Mary Ann Evans**

Like the majority of female writers in the 19th century, Mary Ann Evans used a male pseudonym so that her works would be taken more seriously. Her pen name, [George Eliot, came around 1857](http://www.notablebiographies.com/Du-Fi/Eliot-George.html) when Evans published her first short story titled “Amos Barton.” Evans took the name “George” from philosopher and her lover[George Henry Lewes](https://www.britannica.com/biography/George-Eliot) to whom she never married but lived with until his death. Lewes oversaw Evans’s work and encouraged her to pursue her literary ambitions. Evans crafted her entire literary career and legacy under her pen name.

### ![Image 18: 25](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/25-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)10. [Lewis Caroll](https://www.enotes.com/topics/lewis-carroll)

**Real Name: Charles Lutwidge Dodgson**

Author of [_Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/alices-adventures) and [_Through the Looking-Glass_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/through-looking-glass-lewis-carroll), Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson. As a scholar and instructor at Oxford, Dodgson valued his privacy—especially when it came to his literary works. He [translated the first two parts of his name](http://www.lewiscarroll.org/faq/) (Charles Lutwidge) into Latin, which gave him “Carolus Ludovicus.” He then reversed the order and translated the name back to English, which left him with“Lewis Carroll.”

### ![Image 19: 26](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/26-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)11. Mary Westmacott

**Real Name: [Agatha Mary Clarissa Miller Christie](https://www.enotes.com/topics/agatha-christie)**

Under the pen name Mary Westmacott, Agatha Christie was able to divert from her usual realm of writing [mystery and crime novels](https://www.enotes.com/authors/agatha-christie). The alias allowed Christie to explore writing about human psychology and love without expectations from her already established mystery fan base. Agatha [chose her new name](http://www.agathachristie.com/about-christie/family-memories/the-mary-westmacotts) by combining her middle name (Mary) and the family name of distant relatives (Westmacott). She successfully used the pseudonym for nearly twenty years without revealing her true identity.

### ![Image 20: 27](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/27-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)12. [Voltaire](https://www.enotes.com/topics/voltaire)

**Real Name: François‐Marie Arouet**

With a literary career stretching over 60 years, Voltaire may be one of the most immortal pen names of literature. While the origins of François‐Marie Arouet’s pen name are unclear, it’s been suggested that the adoption of Voltaire was a result of rejecting Arounet’s family name due to a strained relationship with his father. [The most popular theory remains that “Voltaire” was an anagram of a Latinized spelling of “Arouet,”](http://www.history.com/news/10-things-you-should-know-about-voltaire) but others claim it could have been Arouet’s nickname “Voluntaire” (French for “volunteer”), which may have been a sarcastic nod to the writer’s stubbornness.

### ![Image 21: 28](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/28-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)13. [George Orwell](https://www.enotes.com/topics/george-orwell)

**Real Name: Eric Blair**

Before[_Animal Farm_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/animal-farm) and [_1984_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/1984?en_action=search&en_label=top_pick_study_guide&en_category=internal_campaign), Eric Blair published a memoir titled [_Down and Out in Paris and London_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/down-out-paris-london) in 1933. [He adopted the name George Orwell so his family would not be embarrassed](https://www.biography.com/people/george-orwell-9429833) as he recounted his experiences growing up in poverty. Being a fan of English tradition, Blair also felt that Orwell sounded like a reputable British name.

### ![Image 22: 29](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/29-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)14. [Ayn Rand](https://www.enotes.com/topics/ayn-rand)

**Real Name: Alisa Zinov’yevna Rosenbaum**

Author of bestselling books [_The Fountainhead_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/fountainhead) and [_Atlas Shrugged_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/atlas-shrugged), Ayn Rand is known for promoting her philosophy of [Objectivism](https://www.enotes.com/homework-help/philosophy-ayn-rand-relevant-today-395446). Rand adopted her pen name when she moved to the United States to pursue a writing career. Because her family was still living in Soviet Russia, Rand did not want to risk putting her family in danger with her outspoken, and often critical, works.

### ![Image 23: 30](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/30-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)15. [Pablo Neruda](https://www.enotes.com/topics/pablo-neruda)

**Real Name: Ricardo Eliecer Neftalí Reyes Basoalto**

A young Neruda adopted his pen name around 1920 when he started writing for the literary journal “Selva Austral.”[To avoid conflict with his family](https://www.poets.org/poetsorg/poet/pablo-neruda), who disapproved of his occupation, Neruda crafted his alias from the deceased Czechoslovak poet Jan Neruda. [By 1946, Neruda legally changed his name](http://www.encyclopedia.com/people/literature-and-arts/latin-american-literature-biographies/pablo-neruda) to match and embrace the poetic and politically charged identity he had created for himself over the years.

### ![Image 24: 31](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/31-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)16. [Maya Angelou](https://www.enotes.com/topics/maya-angelou)

**Real Name: Marguerite Annie Johnson**

Now a household name, Maya Angelou was born Marguerite Annie Johnson in 1928. [Married briefly to a Greek sailor](https://www.boston.com/news/national-news/2014/05/28/8-things-you-might-not-have-known-about-maya-angelou) named Tosh Angelos, the pen name Maya Angelou was created when the writer combined her nickname (Maya) with an alternative version of her ex-husband’s last name.

### ![Image 25: 32](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/32-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)17. Richard Bachman

**Real Name: [Stephen King](https://www.enotes.com/topics/stephen-king)**

The “King of Horror” has published seven novels under the alias Richard Bachman. Apparently, King came up with the name on a whim while on the phone with his publisher; with a Richard Stark book on his desk and a Bachman–Turner Overdrive song playing in the background, [Richard Bachman was born](http://newsfeed.time.com/2013/07/15/famous-authors-with-secret-pseudonyms/slide/stephen-king-richard-bachmann/). King concealed his true identity for about five years until a [bookstore clerk named Steve Brown](http://mentalfloss.com/article/502166/how-stephen-king-was-outed-richard-bachman) determined that the two authors were the same person. Once the secret was out, King retired Richard Bachman, crediting his death to the “cancer of the pseudonym.”

### ![Image 26: 33](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/33-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)18. [bell hooks](https://www.enotes.com/topics/bell-hooks)

**Real Name: Gloria Jean Watkins**

One of the most prominent feminist voices of our generation, Watkins [derived her pen name from her maternal great-grandmother, Bell Blair Hooks.](http://www.theheroinecollective.com/bell-hooks/) Watkins never capitalizes her pen name in order to preserve and honor the memory of her great-grandmother; a women she admired for her sharp opinions. Watkins established a reputation of a woman that [“talked back”](http://www.notablebiographies.com/He-Ho/Hooks-Bell.html), for she was not afraid to speak up against the injustice she experienced in everyday life. She first used her pen name to publish a short book of poetry and made the grammatical decision to never capitalize the name in order to [place the focus solely on her writing](http://www.theheroinecollective.com/bell-hooks/) rather than the person behind it.

### ![Image 27: 34](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/34-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)19. Lemony Snicket

**Real Name: Daniel Handler**

Lemony Snicket is both the author and the narrator of Handler’s[_A Series of Unfortunate Events_](https://www.enotes.com/homework-help/topic/series-unfortunate); essentially, Lemony Snicket is Handler’s alter ego. During public appearances, Handler will introduce himself as Snicket’s representative explaining to the audience that the real author [could not be in attendance due to some unforeseen disaster](http://www.notablebiographies.com/news/Sh-Z/Snicket-Lemony-Daniel-Handler.html).

### ![Image 28: 35](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/35-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)20. [J.K. Rowling & Robert Galbrath](https://www.enotes.com/topics/j-k-rowling)

**Real Name: Joanne Rowling**

The bestselling author of the [_Harry Potter_ series](https://www.enotes.com/topics/harry-potter-novels) has adopted a few different pen names throughout the course of her career. Originally, publishers feared young boys would not be inclined to read her series once they saw it was published by a female author. Rowling, who has no middle name, took the “K” from her grandmother’s name, Kathleen. As a dynamic writer, Rowling ventured into writing crime fiction where she adopted the [pseudonym Robert Galbraith](http://robert-galbraith.com/about/) to release new work without hype or expectation. In fact, no one had any idea Rowling was Galbraith until an investigation into [forensic linguistics led by England’s _Sunday Times_](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/how-did-computers-uncover-jk-rowlings-pseudonym-180949824/) revealed an extremely similar writing style between the author’s works.

### ![Image 29: 36](https://i0.wp.com/blog.enotes.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/02/36-1.png?resize=600%2C600&ssl=1)21. E.L. James

**Real Name: Erika Leonard**

The British author of the bestselling _Fifty Shades of Grey_ series initially used the pen name [“Snowqueens Icedragon”](http://www.newsweek.com/unassuming-creator-behind-fifty-shades-grey-306676) in an online [_Twilight_](https://www.enotes.com/topics/twilight) fan-fiction forum where she first showcased an early version of _Fifty Shades of Grey_ titled _[Master of the Universe](http://www.adweek.com/galleycat/fifty-shades-of-grey-wayback-machine/50128)_. Once Leonard’s works started gaining popularity and she began transitioning to print, she adopted a new pen name that, in her opinion, was a little more professional. E.L. James was derived from Leonard’s family name (James) plus her first and middle initial. Ultimately, Leonard’s use of a pseudonym granted her the ability to keep her success as an erotic romance author separate from her soft-spoken, housewife reality.

* * *

Choosing a pen name is sometimes more than just a marketing strategy, and there are many ways an author decides on a pen name to embody the essence of their chosen alias. As we’ve seen as well, the majority of writers adapt them from their birth names—using abbreviations, translations from foreign languages, or variations of nicknames—to mark a personal claim on their chosen pseudonym. Regardless of why or how writers choose their _noms de plume_, there is no right or wrong way to go about it, for the work is bound to speak for itself.

There are several [pen-name generators](https://www.name-generator.org.uk/) sprinkled about the internet that provide witty and humorous suggestions for contemporary writers. Tell us what your pen name would be!

Scrooge. Alice. Holmes. The Wicked Witch. Dracula. Father Brown. Peter Rabbit and a whole lot of other familiar characters were created by individuals who either alive in 1889 or had relatives alive in 1889. Most of these books are now in the public domain. This is why Wicked exists. This is why several low budget horror movies exist like Winnie the Pooh: Blood and Honey and Popeye the Slayer Man because their copyright has expired and anybody can use them in anyway they want. As of 1925 all literature published before 1930 is now up for grabs to use in your own creations. Here are just some of those authors who existed at the same time as other famous authors 11 years before the start of the 20th century giving us lots of stories to read and use. Some of them like Ben Hur bringing Christian ideas we can enjoy and share.

## Born in 18th Century

## Jane Austen’s Nephews

### Descendants of Some Famous People Not Alive in 1889

[George Austen](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Austen-109)(1731-1805) was the father of  
[Jane Austen –](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Austen)(December 16, 1775 –July 18, 1817)  
 And her brother [Francis William Austen](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Austen-497)(1774-1865) who was the father of  
 Jane’s nephew [George Austen](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Austen-1777)(bef.1812-1903) who was the father of  
 Jane’s great nephew [Ernest Leigh Austen](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Austen-1833)(1859-1939)

![Image 12](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/09/CassandraAusten-JaneAustenc.1810_hires-233x300.jpg)

**Jane Austen** was an English novelist known primarily for her six novels, which implicitly interpret, critique, and comment upon the British[landed gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landed_gentry)at the end of the 18th century. Austen’s plots often explore the dependence of women on marriage for the pursuit of favourable social standing and economic security. Her works are implicit critiques of the[novels of sensibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_novel)of the second half of the 18th century and are part of the transition to 19th-century[literary realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_realism). Her use of social commentary, realism, and irony have earned her acclaim amongst critics and scholars.

The anonymously published _[Sense and Sensibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense\_and\_Sensibility)_(1811),_[Pride and Prejudice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride\_and\_Prejudice)_(1813),_[Mansfield Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield\_Park)_(1814), and _[Emma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma\_(novel))_(1816) were modest successes, but they brought her little fame in her lifetime. She wrote two other novels—_[Northanger Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northanger\_Abbey)_ and _[Persuasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persuasion\_(novel))_, both published posthumously in 1817—and began another, eventually titled _[Sanditon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanditon)_, but it was left unfinished upon her death. She also left behind three volumes of juvenile writings in manuscript, the short[epistolary novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistolary_novel)_[Lady Susan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady\_Susan)_, and the unfinished novel _[The Watsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Watsons)_.

Since her death Austen’s novels have rarely been out of print. A significant transition in her reputation occurred in 1833, when they were republished in[Richard Bentley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bentley_(publisher))‘s Standard Novels series (illustrated by Ferdinand Pickering and sold as a set). They gradually gained wide acclaim and popular readership. In 1869, fifty-two years after her death, her nephew’s publication of _[A Memoir of Jane Austen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Memoir\_of\_Jane\_Austen)_ introduced a compelling version of her writing career and her supposedly uneventful life to an eager audience. Her work has inspired a large number of critical essays and has been included in many literary anthologies. Her novels have also inspired many films, including 1940’s _[Pride and Prejudice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride\_and\_Prejudice\_(1940\_film))_, 1995’s _[Sense and Sensibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense\_and\_Sensibility\_(film))_, and 2016’s _[Love & Friendship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love\_%26\_Friendship)_.

![Image 13](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/09/Prideundprejudice-198x300.jpg)

In 1977

[A little bit of ivory : a life of Jane Austen](https://archive.org/details/littlebitofivory0000vipo) is published

by [Elfrida Vipont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elfrida_Vipont)  
 (July 3, 1902 – March 14, 1992)

She was an English writer of children’s literature. She was born in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester")into a family of[Quakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers "Quakers"). As a children’s writer, she initially published under a man’s name,**Charles Vipont**, which was a common marketing device by publishers at the time.She later wrote as**Elfrida Vipont**, and after her marriage sometimes as**E. V. Foulds**. She was also a schoolteacher and a prominent Quaker.

In 2022

[Jane & Me: My Austen Heritage](https://www.amazon.com/Jane-Me-My-Austen-Heritage-ebook/dp/B0B8LZ8DX2/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1JA59R4K7NCFP&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.EHxbU927_w7U2JTZKAz_Q-usp2gpPhWAA-KvKo_jIeLizs1jhsgtSV0C4xcFr9L5ipC5NIxE3niXvmw8TXD23tEfW4kqQr3XvgVUMPjk4SnWGOXIaUh60WmVMCkdHARt4GIk9IHiR_ePn28aYkRvttBgMjwQ9IVoDufkKc7q6F37yNKjlOCop89FStexIJGXJf9PDdri7YiuAtcLQhplXMHi65M7duTKjI0DdmsULCY.LdXljzforisJrO25wzUgYuMsnpQnW7RueTv-dLilAxE&dib_tag=se&keywords=Jane+and+me&qid=1731029906&sprefix=jane+and+m%2Caps%2C411&sr=8-1) by[Caroline Knight](https://www.amazon.com/Caroline-Knight/e/B0748K5YJ4/ref=dp_byline_cont_ebooks_1) (born ab. 1970)

is published.

> _Caroline Jane Knight shares more than Jane Austen’s name and DNA. As a direct descendant of Jane’s brother, Edward Knight, Caroline is the last of the Austen Knight family to grow up at Chawton House on the estate where Jane Austen lived and enjoyed the most productive period of her writing career. Caroline explored the same places around Chawton House and its grounds as Jane did, dined at the same table in the same dining room, read in the same library and shared the same dream of independence. Caroline’s early life was filled with the delights of living in a sixteenth-century English manor, the good cheer of family gatherings and centuries-old Christmas traditions in the Great Hall of Chawton House, the beauty of a country life, and the joys of helping her Granny bake cakes and serve Jane Austen devotees in the Chawton House tea room. But when she was seventeen, Caroline and her family were forced to leave the home her family had lived in for centuries. Heartbroken, but determined to leave all things Austen behind her, Caroline eventually carved out a highly successful career in business. This is the story of Caroline’s tumultuous journey to success, her ultimate crisis, her rediscovery and embrace of her Austen heritage, and the creation of the Jane Austen Literacy Foundation.- Amazon Description_

## Born in 1800’s

[**Catharine Parr Traill**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catharine_Parr_Traill)(January 9, 1802 –August 29, 1899)

Catharine wrote [The Canadian Crusoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Crusoes) (1852) Considered the first Canadian novel for children.

![Image 15](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/Catharine_Parr_Traill-195x300.jpg)

[John Greenleaf Whittier](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fen.m.wikipedia.org%2Fwiki%2FJohn_Greenleaf_Whittier%3Ffbclid%3DIwZXh0bgNhZW0CMTAAAR0BF9d6Z8i0Lc5qQBXWc4rMn7v_rgSB68Jwc9lBUCcOejGVfOWBHW1dM-s_aem_PjTOKWUnVapCwTRA40dZQA&h=AT1q8qVV81MfFMaAdTXbWYVIE6SjtjQyZVPjno8DVQlTzaszCCL6h64DM7ihkXydxH-aMFt0dxA4m8PDk2uLkwB7Nvqpy8sx9wZr7dJT--xZlq_W1DPP2l0JrUp9HIf5eIRreG6rLRgafqRu8tYc1Qh1gIDVgA&__tn__=R%5d-R&c%5b0%5d=AT2r7annfIRKQwM7WpZm0cX1D2jnlDolOBJawzv0Pi3f4FyA88ywhnwgIqv1_KPosOYJ47KF7OFqZlOs3xj0bymIGaj6Ma7zsy3LnBZqZLtkOKPKLu8ttfYO2JnjuA56h2BXD6mUoPDog6pGR-ljdY_XFbshJy9h6fYH57ez3xoA5agGVfjjig)  
 (December 17, 1807 – September 7, 1892)

He was an American [Quaker](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers)poet and advocate of the[abolition](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States)of[slavery in the United States](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States). Frequently listed as one of the[fireside poets](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireside_poets), he was influenced by the Scottish poet[Robert Burns](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Burns). Whittier is remembered particularly for his anti-slavery writings, as well as his 1866 book[_Snow-Bound_](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow-Bound).

![Image 16](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/Snow-Bound_1866_title_page_large-174x300.jpg)

[Alfred, Lord Tennyson](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred,_Lord_Tennyson)  
 (August 6, 1809 – October 6, 1892)

He was an English poet. He was the [Poet Laureate](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate_of_the_United_Kingdom)during much of[Queen Victoria](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria)‘s reign. In 1829, Tennyson was awarded the[Chancellor’s Gold Medal](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor%27s_Gold_Medal)at Cambridge for one of his first pieces, “Timbuktu”. He published his first solo collection of poems,[_Poems, Chiefly Lyrical_](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poems,_Chiefly_Lyrical), in 1830. “[Claribel](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claribel_(poem))” and “[Mariana](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_(poem))“, which remain some of Tennyson’s most celebrated poems, were included in this volume. Although described by some critics as overly sentimental, his poems ultimately proved popular and brought Tennyson to the attention of well-known writers of the day, including[Samuel Taylor Coleridge](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge). Tennyson’s early poetry, with its medievalism and powerful visual imagery, was a major influence on the[Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Raphaelite_Brotherhood).

![Image 17](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/Alfred_Lord_Tennyson_by_Elliott__Fry_-_Original-191x300.jpg)

[Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Wendell_Holmes_Sr.)  
 (August 29, 1809 – October 7, 1894)

He was an American physician, poet, and [polymath](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymath "Polymath")based in Boston. Grouped among the[fireside poets](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireside_poets "Fireside poets"), he was acclaimed by his peers as one of the best writers of the day. His most famous prose works are the “Breakfast-Table” series, which began with _[The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Autocrat\_of\_the\_Breakfast-Table "The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table")_(1858). He was also an important medical reformer. In addition to his work as an author and poet, Holmes also served as a physician, professor, lecturer, inventor, and, although he never practiced it, he received formal training in law.

![Image 18](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/Oliver_Wendell_Holmes_Sr_c1879.jpg)

## Born in 1810’s

[**Harriet Beecher Stowe**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Beecher_Stowe)  
 (American) (June 14, 1811 – July 1, 1896)

She was an American author and [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States "Abolitionism in the United States"). She came from the religious[Beecher family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beecher_family "Beecher family")and wrote the popular novel _[Uncle Tom’s Cabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle\_Tom%27s\_Cabin "Uncle Tom's Cabin")_(1852), which depicts the harsh conditions experienced by[enslaved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States")[African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans"). The book reached an audience of millions as a novel and play, and became influential in the United States and in[Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland"), energizing anti-slavery forces in the[American North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_United_States "Northern United States"), while provoking widespread anger in the[South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antebellum_South "Antebellum South"). Stowe wrote 30 books, including novels, three travel memoirs, and collections of articles and letters. She was influential both for her writings as well as for her public stances and debates on social issues of the day.

![Image 19](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/220px-Beecher-Stowe-210x300.jpg)

## James Fenimore Cooper’s Wife

[James Fenimore Cooper](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fenimore_Cooper)  
 (September 15, 1789 – September 14, 1851)

He was an American writer of the first half of the 19th century, whose [historical romances](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_romances "Historical romances")depicting colonial and indigenous characters from the 17th to the 19th centuries brought him fame and fortune. He lived much of his boyhood and his last fifteen years in[Cooperstown, New York](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperstown,_New_York "Cooperstown, New York"), which was founded by his father[William Cooper](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cooper_(judge) "William Cooper (judge)")on property that he owned. Cooper became a member of the[Episcopal Church](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)")shortly before his death and contributed generously to it. He attended[Yale University](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")for three years, where he was a member of the[Linonian Society](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linonian_Society "Linonian Society").

His best-known works are five[historical novels](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_novel "Historical novel")of the frontier period, written between 1823 and 1841, known as the _[Leatherstocking Tales](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherstocking\_Tales "Leatherstocking Tales")_, which introduced the iconic American frontier scout,[Natty Bumppo](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natty_Bumppo "Natty Bumppo"). Cooper’s works on the U.S. Navy have been well received among naval historians, but they were sometimes criticized by his contemporaries. Among his more famous works is the[Romantic](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism")novel _[The Last of the Mohicans](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_of\_the\_Mohicans "The Last of the Mohicans")_, often regarded as his[masterpiece](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masterpiece "Masterpiece").

![Image 20](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/The_Last_of_the_Mohicans_FilmPoster-197x300.jpeg)

He was the husband of

[Susan Fenimore Cooper](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Fenimore_Cooper)  
 (April 17, 1813– December 31, 1894)

She was an American writer and amateur [naturalist](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalist "Naturalist"). She founded an orphanage in[Cooperstown, New York](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperstown,_New_York "Cooperstown, New York")and made it a successful charity. The daughter of writer[James Fenimore Cooper](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fenimore_Cooper "James Fenimore Cooper"), she served as his secretary and[amanuensis](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanuensis "Amanuensis")late in his life.

## Charlotte Brontë’s Husband

(April 21, 1816 –March 31, 1855)

She was an English novelist and poet, the eldest of the three [Brontë sisters](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bront%C3%AB_family "Brontë family")who survived into adulthood and whose novels became classics of[English literature](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_literature "English literature").  (November 11, 1821 – February 9, 1881),

He was a Russian novelist, short story writer, essayist and journalist. Numerous literary critics regard him as one of the greatest novelists in all of [world literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_literature "World literature"), as many of his works are considered highly influential masterpieces.Dostoevsky’s literary works explore the[human condition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_condition "Human condition")in the troubled political, social, and spiritual atmospheres of[19th-century Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire"), and engage with a variety of philosophical and religious themes. His most acclaimed novels include _[Crime and Punishment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime\_and\_Punishment "Crime and Punishment")_(1866),_[The Idiot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Idiot "The Idiot")_(1869),[_Demons_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demons_(Dostoevsky_novel) "Demons (Dostoevsky novel)")(1872),[_The Adolescent_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Adolescent "The Adolescent")(1875), and _[The Brothers Karamazov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Brothers\_Karamazov "The Brothers Karamazov")_(1880). His 1864[novella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novella "Novella")_[Notes from Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notes\_from\_Underground "Notes from Underground")_ is considered to be one of the first works of[existentialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existentialism "Existentialism")literature.

[Lyubov Dostoevskaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyubov_Dostoevskaya)  
 (September 14, 1869 – November 10, 1926)

She was a Russian writer and [memoirist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoirist "Memoirist"). Lyubov Dostoevskaya is best known for the book _Dostoyevsky as Portrayed by His Daughter_ also known as _Dostoyevsky According to His Daughter_), originally published in[Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich")in 1920. Her memoirs, written in French and published in German, were later translated into other[European languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_languages "European languages"). In 1920 the book was released in[Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language")(in[Arnhem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnhem "Arnhem")), the following year there were translations into[Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language")and English, and in 1922 it was published in the United States and Italy.A Russian version, highly abridged, was published in 1922 by Gosudarstvennoe Izdatelstvo ([Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg "Saint Petersburg")) under the title “Достоевский в изображении его дочери Л. Достоевской”.

The work contains many factual inaccuracies, partly because Lyubov was only 11 at the time of her father’s death, and partly because she based the memoirs on her mother’s stories. Many researchers tend to see this memoir as subjective and unreliable, citing as an example her bias in the description of the relationship between Dostoevsky and his first wife, Mariya Isayeva.Both Lyubov and her mother Anna expressed hatred towards Isayeva.

_The Young Fur-Traders_(1856),_[The Coral Island](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Coral\_Island "The Coral Island")_(1857),_The World of Ice_(1859),_Ungava: a Tale of Eskimo Land_(1857),_The Dog Crusoe_(1860),_The Lighthouse_(1865),_Fighting the Whales_(1866),_Deep Down_(1868),_[The Pirate City](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pirate\_City:\_An\_Algerine\_Tale "The Pirate City: An Algerine Tale")_(1874),_Erling the Bold_(1869),_The Settler and the Savage_(1877), and more than 100 other books followed in regular succession, his rule being to write as far as possible from personal knowledge of the scenes he described. _[The Gorilla Hunters. _The Coral Island_ is the most popular of the Ballantyne novels still read and remembered today,but because of one mistake he made in that book, in which he gave an incorrect thickness of coconut shells, he subsequently attempted to gain first-hand knowledge of his subject matter. For instance, he spent some time living with the lighthouse keepers at the[Bell Rock](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Rock_Lighthouse "Bell Rock Lighthouse")before writing _The Lighthouse_, and while researching for _Deep Down_ he spent time with the[tin miners](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin_mining "Tin mining")of[Cornwall](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall "Cornwall").

 (January 1, 1839– January 25, 1908),

Going by the name **Marie Louise de la Ramée**and known by the[pseudonym](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudonym "Pseudonym")**Ouida**wrote more than 40 novels, as well as short stories, children’s books and essays. Moderately successful, she lived a life of luxury, entertaining many of the literary figures of the day.

_[Under Two Flags](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under\_Two\_Flags\_(novel))_(1867), one of her most famous novels, described the British in[Algeria](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria "Algeria"). It expressed sympathy for the French colonists – with whom Ouida deeply identified – and, to some extent, the[Arabs](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs"). The novel was adapted for the stage, and was filmed six times. Her 1872 novel _[A Dog of Flanders](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Dog\_of\_Flanders "A Dog of Flanders")_ is considered a children’s classic in much of[Asia](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia"). The American author [Jack London](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_London "Jack London")cited her novel _Signa_ as one of the reasons for his literary success. Her lavish lifestyle eventually led her to penury, and her works were put up for auction to pay her debts. She died in Italy from[pneumonia](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia"). Soon after her death, her friends organized a public subscription in[Bury St Edmunds](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bury_St_Edmunds "Bury St Edmunds"), her birthplace, where they had a fountain for horses and dogs installed in her name.

He was a German-born American [caricaturist](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caricaturist)and[editorial cartoonist](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Editorial_cartoonist) often considered to be the “Father of the American Cartoon”.

Nast was associated with the magazine[_Harper’s Weekly_](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harper%27s_Weekly)from 1859 to 1860 and from 1862 until 1886. Nast’s influence was so widespread that[Theodore Roosevelt](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Roosevelt)once said, “Thomas Nast was our best teacher.”

[**Henry James**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_James)(American)  
 (April 15, 1843 – February 28,1916)

He was an American-British author. He is regarded as a key transitional figure between [literary realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_realism "Literary realism")and[literary modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_modernism "Literary modernism"), and is considered by many to be among the greatest novelists in the English language. He was the son of[Henry James Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_James_Sr. "Henry James Sr.")and the brother of philosopher and psychologist[William James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_James "William James")and diarist[Alice James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_James "Alice James").

He is best known for his novels dealing with the social and marital interplay between _émigré_ Americans, the English, and continental Europeans, such as _[The Portrait of a Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Portrait\_of\_a\_Lady "The Portrait of a Lady")_. His later works, such as _[The Ambassadors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ambassadors "The Ambassadors")_,_[The Wings of the Dove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wings\_of\_the\_Dove "The Wings of the Dove")_ and _[The Golden Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Golden\_Bowl "The Golden Bowl")_ were increasingly experimental. In describing the internal states of mind and social dynamics of his characters, James often wrote in a style in which ambiguous or contradictory motives and impressions were overlaid or juxtaposed in the discussion of a character’s psyche. For their unique ambiguity, as well as for other aspects of their composition, his late works have been compared to[Impressionist painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism").

His novella _[The Turn of the Screw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Turn\_of\_the\_Screw "The Turn of the Screw")_ has garnered a reputation as the most analysed and ambiguous[ghost story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_story "Ghost story")in the English language and remains his most widely adapted work in other media. He wrote other highly regarded ghost stories, such as “[The Jolly Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jolly_Corner "The Jolly Corner")“.

Scrooge. Alice. Holmes. The Wicked Witch. Dracula. Father Brown. Peter Rabbit and a whole lot of other familiar characters were created by individuals who either alive in 1889 or had relatives alive in 1889. Most of these books are now in the public domain. This is why Wicked exists. This is why several low budget horror movies exist like Winnie the Pooh: Blood and Honey and Popeye the Slayer Man because their copyright has expired and anybody can use them in anyway they want. As of 1925 all literature published before 1930 is now up for grabs to use in your own creations. Here are just some of those authors who existed at the same time as other famous authors 11 years before the start of the 20th century giving us lots of stories to read and use. Some of them like Ben Hur bringing Christian ideas we can enjoy and share.

## Born in 18th Century

## Jane Austen’s Nephews

### Descendants of Some Famous People Not Alive in 1889

[George Austen](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Austen-109)(1731-1805) was the father of  
[Jane Austen –](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Austen)(December 16, 1775 –July 18, 1817)  
 And her brother [Francis William Austen](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Austen-497)(1774-1865) who was the father of  
 Jane’s nephew [George Austen](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Austen-1777)(bef.1812-1903) who was the father of  
 Jane’s great nephew [Ernest Leigh Austen](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Austen-1833)(1859-1939)

![Image 12](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/09/CassandraAusten-JaneAustenc.1810_hires-233x300.jpg)

**Jane Austen** was an English novelist known primarily for her six novels, which implicitly interpret, critique, and comment upon the British[landed gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landed_gentry)at the end of the 18th century. Austen’s plots often explore the dependence of women on marriage for the pursuit of favourable social standing and economic security. Her works are implicit critiques of the[novels of sensibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sentimental_novel)of the second half of the 18th century and are part of the transition to 19th-century[literary realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_realism). Her use of social commentary, realism, and irony have earned her acclaim amongst critics and scholars.

The anonymously published _[Sense and Sensibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense\_and\_Sensibility)_(1811),_[Pride and Prejudice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride\_and\_Prejudice)_(1813),_[Mansfield Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield\_Park)_(1814), and _[Emma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma\_(novel))_(1816) were modest successes, but they brought her little fame in her lifetime. She wrote two other novels—_[Northanger Abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northanger\_Abbey)_ and _[Persuasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persuasion\_(novel))_, both published posthumously in 1817—and began another, eventually titled _[Sanditon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanditon)_, but it was left unfinished upon her death. She also left behind three volumes of juvenile writings in manuscript, the short[epistolary novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epistolary_novel)_[Lady Susan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady\_Susan)_, and the unfinished novel _[The Watsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Watsons)_.

Since her death Austen’s novels have rarely been out of print. A significant transition in her reputation occurred in 1833, when they were republished in[Richard Bentley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bentley_(publisher))‘s Standard Novels series (illustrated by Ferdinand Pickering and sold as a set). They gradually gained wide acclaim and popular readership. In 1869, fifty-two years after her death, her nephew’s publication of _[A Memoir of Jane Austen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Memoir\_of\_Jane\_Austen)_ introduced a compelling version of her writing career and her supposedly uneventful life to an eager audience. Her work has inspired a large number of critical essays and has been included in many literary anthologies. Her novels have also inspired many films, including 1940’s _[Pride and Prejudice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pride\_and\_Prejudice\_(1940\_film))_, 1995’s _[Sense and Sensibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense\_and\_Sensibility\_(film))_, and 2016’s _[Love & Friendship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love\_%26\_Friendship)_.

![Image 13](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/09/Prideundprejudice-198x300.jpg)

In 1977

[A little bit of ivory : a life of Jane Austen](https://archive.org/details/littlebitofivory0000vipo) is published

by [Elfrida Vipont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elfrida_Vipont)  
 (July 3, 1902 – March 14, 1992)

She was an English writer of children’s literature. She was born in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester")into a family of[Quakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers "Quakers"). As a children’s writer, she initially published under a man’s name,**Charles Vipont**, which was a common marketing device by publishers at the time.She later wrote as**Elfrida Vipont**, and after her marriage sometimes as**E. V. Foulds**. She was also a schoolteacher and a prominent Quaker.

In 2022

[Jane & Me: My Austen Heritage](https://www.amazon.com/Jane-Me-My-Austen-Heritage-ebook/dp/B0B8LZ8DX2/ref=sr_1_1?crid=1JA59R4K7NCFP&dib=eyJ2IjoiMSJ9.EHxbU927_w7U2JTZKAz_Q-usp2gpPhWAA-KvKo_jIeLizs1jhsgtSV0C4xcFr9L5ipC5NIxE3niXvmw8TXD23tEfW4kqQr3XvgVUMPjk4SnWGOXIaUh60WmVMCkdHARt4GIk9IHiR_ePn28aYkRvttBgMjwQ9IVoDufkKc7q6F37yNKjlOCop89FStexIJGXJf9PDdri7YiuAtcLQhplXMHi65M7duTKjI0DdmsULCY.LdXljzforisJrO25wzUgYuMsnpQnW7RueTv-dLilAxE&dib_tag=se&keywords=Jane+and+me&qid=1731029906&sprefix=jane+and+m%2Caps%2C411&sr=8-1) by[Caroline Knight](https://www.amazon.com/Caroline-Knight/e/B0748K5YJ4/ref=dp_byline_cont_ebooks_1) (born ab. 1970)

is published.

> _Caroline Jane Knight shares more than Jane Austen’s name and DNA. As a direct descendant of Jane’s brother, Edward Knight, Caroline is the last of the Austen Knight family to grow up at Chawton House on the estate where Jane Austen lived and enjoyed the most productive period of her writing career. Caroline explored the same places around Chawton House and its grounds as Jane did, dined at the same table in the same dining room, read in the same library and shared the same dream of independence. Caroline’s early life was filled with the delights of living in a sixteenth-century English manor, the good cheer of family gatherings and centuries-old Christmas traditions in the Great Hall of Chawton House, the beauty of a country life, and the joys of helping her Granny bake cakes and serve Jane Austen devotees in the Chawton House tea room. But when she was seventeen, Caroline and her family were forced to leave the home her family had lived in for centuries. Heartbroken, but determined to leave all things Austen behind her, Caroline eventually carved out a highly successful career in business. This is the story of Caroline’s tumultuous journey to success, her ultimate crisis, her rediscovery and embrace of her Austen heritage, and the creation of the Jane Austen Literacy Foundation.- Amazon Description_

## Born in 1800’s

[**Catharine Parr Traill**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catharine_Parr_Traill)(January 9, 1802 –August 29, 1899)

Catharine wrote [The Canadian Crusoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Crusoes) (1852) Considered the first Canadian novel for children.

![Image 15](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/Catharine_Parr_Traill-195x300.jpg)

[John Greenleaf Whittier](https://l.facebook.com/l.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fen.m.wikipedia.org%2Fwiki%2FJohn_Greenleaf_Whittier%3Ffbclid%3DIwZXh0bgNhZW0CMTAAAR0BF9d6Z8i0Lc5qQBXWc4rMn7v_rgSB68Jwc9lBUCcOejGVfOWBHW1dM-s_aem_PjTOKWUnVapCwTRA40dZQA&h=AT1q8qVV81MfFMaAdTXbWYVIE6SjtjQyZVPjno8DVQlTzaszCCL6h64DM7ihkXydxH-aMFt0dxA4m8PDk2uLkwB7Nvqpy8sx9wZr7dJT--xZlq_W1DPP2l0JrUp9HIf5eIRreG6rLRgafqRu8tYc1Qh1gIDVgA&__tn__=R%5d-R&c%5b0%5d=AT2r7annfIRKQwM7WpZm0cX1D2jnlDolOBJawzv0Pi3f4FyA88ywhnwgIqv1_KPosOYJ47KF7OFqZlOs3xj0bymIGaj6Ma7zsy3LnBZqZLtkOKPKLu8ttfYO2JnjuA56h2BXD6mUoPDog6pGR-ljdY_XFbshJy9h6fYH57ez3xoA5agGVfjjig)  
 (December 17, 1807 – September 7, 1892)

He was an American [Quaker](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers)poet and advocate of the[abolition](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States)of[slavery in the United States](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States). Frequently listed as one of the[fireside poets](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireside_poets), he was influenced by the Scottish poet[Robert Burns](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Burns). Whittier is remembered particularly for his anti-slavery writings, as well as his 1866 book[_Snow-Bound_](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow-Bound).

![Image 16](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/Snow-Bound_1866_title_page_large-174x300.jpg)

[Alfred, Lord Tennyson](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred,_Lord_Tennyson)  
 (August 6, 1809 – October 6, 1892)

He was an English poet. He was the [Poet Laureate](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poet_Laureate_of_the_United_Kingdom)during much of[Queen Victoria](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Victoria)‘s reign. In 1829, Tennyson was awarded the[Chancellor’s Gold Medal](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor%27s_Gold_Medal)at Cambridge for one of his first pieces, “Timbuktu”. He published his first solo collection of poems,[_Poems, Chiefly Lyrical_](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poems,_Chiefly_Lyrical), in 1830. “[Claribel](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claribel_(poem))” and “[Mariana](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariana_(poem))“, which remain some of Tennyson’s most celebrated poems, were included in this volume. Although described by some critics as overly sentimental, his poems ultimately proved popular and brought Tennyson to the attention of well-known writers of the day, including[Samuel Taylor Coleridge](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Taylor_Coleridge). Tennyson’s early poetry, with its medievalism and powerful visual imagery, was a major influence on the[Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-Raphaelite_Brotherhood).

![Image 17](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/Alfred_Lord_Tennyson_by_Elliott__Fry_-_Original-191x300.jpg)

[Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oliver_Wendell_Holmes_Sr.)  
 (August 29, 1809 – October 7, 1894)

He was an American physician, poet, and [polymath](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polymath "Polymath")based in Boston. Grouped among the[fireside poets](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fireside_poets "Fireside poets"), he was acclaimed by his peers as one of the best writers of the day. His most famous prose works are the “Breakfast-Table” series, which began with _[The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Autocrat\_of\_the\_Breakfast-Table "The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table")_(1858). He was also an important medical reformer. In addition to his work as an author and poet, Holmes also served as a physician, professor, lecturer, inventor, and, although he never practiced it, he received formal training in law.

![Image 18](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/Oliver_Wendell_Holmes_Sr_c1879.jpg)

## Born in 1810’s

[**Harriet Beecher Stowe**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Beecher_Stowe)  
 (American) (June 14, 1811 – July 1, 1896)

She was an American author and [abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionism_in_the_United_States "Abolitionism in the United States"). She came from the religious[Beecher family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beecher_family "Beecher family")and wrote the popular novel _[Uncle Tom’s Cabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uncle\_Tom%27s\_Cabin "Uncle Tom's Cabin")_(1852), which depicts the harsh conditions experienced by[enslaved](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States")[African Americans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans "African Americans"). The book reached an audience of millions as a novel and play, and became influential in the United States and in[Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland"), energizing anti-slavery forces in the[American North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_United_States "Northern United States"), while provoking widespread anger in the[South](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antebellum_South "Antebellum South"). Stowe wrote 30 books, including novels, three travel memoirs, and collections of articles and letters. She was influential both for her writings as well as for her public stances and debates on social issues of the day.

![Image 19](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/220px-Beecher-Stowe-210x300.jpg)

## James Fenimore Cooper’s Wife

[James Fenimore Cooper](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fenimore_Cooper)  
 (September 15, 1789 – September 14, 1851)

He was an American writer of the first half of the 19th century, whose [historical romances](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_romances "Historical romances")depicting colonial and indigenous characters from the 17th to the 19th centuries brought him fame and fortune. He lived much of his boyhood and his last fifteen years in[Cooperstown, New York](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperstown,_New_York "Cooperstown, New York"), which was founded by his father[William Cooper](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Cooper_(judge) "William Cooper (judge)")on property that he owned. Cooper became a member of the[Episcopal Church](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Episcopal_Church_(United_States) "Episcopal Church (United States)")shortly before his death and contributed generously to it. He attended[Yale University](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")for three years, where he was a member of the[Linonian Society](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linonian_Society "Linonian Society").

His best-known works are five[historical novels](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_novel "Historical novel")of the frontier period, written between 1823 and 1841, known as the _[Leatherstocking Tales](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leatherstocking\_Tales "Leatherstocking Tales")_, which introduced the iconic American frontier scout,[Natty Bumppo](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natty_Bumppo "Natty Bumppo"). Cooper’s works on the U.S. Navy have been well received among naval historians, but they were sometimes criticized by his contemporaries. Among his more famous works is the[Romantic](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism")novel _[The Last of the Mohicans](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_of\_the\_Mohicans "The Last of the Mohicans")_, often regarded as his[masterpiece](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masterpiece "Masterpiece").

![Image 20](https://wp-media.patheos.com/blogs/sites/1316/2024/12/The_Last_of_the_Mohicans_FilmPoster-197x300.jpeg)

He was the husband of

[Susan Fenimore Cooper](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Fenimore_Cooper)  
 (April 17, 1813– December 31, 1894)

She was an American writer and amateur [naturalist](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naturalist "Naturalist"). She founded an orphanage in[Cooperstown, New York](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cooperstown,_New_York "Cooperstown, New York")and made it a successful charity. The daughter of writer[James Fenimore Cooper](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Fenimore_Cooper "James Fenimore Cooper"), she served as his secretary and[amanuensis](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amanuensis "Amanuensis")late in his life.

## Charlotte Brontë’s Husband

(April 21, 1816 –March 31, 1855)

She was an English novelist and poet, the eldest of the three [Brontë sisters](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bront%C3%AB_family "Brontë family")who survived into adulthood and whose novels became classics of[English literature](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_literature "English literature"). She is best known for her novel _[Jane Eyre](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane\_Eyre "Jane Eyre")_, which she published under the male pseudonym**Currer Bell**._Jane Eyre_ went on to become a success in publication, and is widely held in high regard in the[gothic fiction](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_fiction "Gothic fiction") genre of literature.

National Portrait Gallery, London

She was the wife of

**Arthur Bell Nicholls**  
 (January 6, 1819 – December 2, 1906)

He was the husband of the English novelist [Charlotte Brontë](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Bront%C3%AB "Charlotte Brontë"). His 1864[novella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novella "Novella")_[Notes from Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notes\_from\_Underground "Notes from Underground")_ is considered to be one of the first works of[existentialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existentialism "Existentialism")literature.

[Lyubov Dostoevskaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyubov_Dostoevskaya)  
 (September 14, 1869 – November 10, 1926)

She was a Russian writer and [memoirist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memoirist "Memoirist"). Lyubov Dostoevskaya is best known for the book _Dostoyevsky as Portrayed by His Daughter_ also known as _Dostoyevsky According to His Daughter_), originally published in[Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich")in 1920. Her memoirs, written in French and published in German, were later translated into other[European languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_languages "European languages"). In 1920 the book was released in[Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language")(in[Arnhem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arnhem "Arnhem")), the following year there were translations into[Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language")and English, and in 1922 it was published in the United States and Italy.A Russian version, highly abridged, was published in 1922 by Gosudarstvennoe Izdatelstvo ([Saint Petersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg "Saint Petersburg")) under the title “Достоевский в изображении его дочери Л. Достоевской”.

The work contains many factual inaccuracies, partly because Lyubov was only 11 at the time of her father’s death, and partly because she based the memoirs on her mother’s stories. Many researchers tend to see this memoir as subjective and unreliable, citing as an example her bias in the description of the relationship between Dostoevsky and his first wife, Mariya Isayeva.Both Lyubov and her mother Anna expressed hatred towards Isayeva.

_The Young Fur-Traders_(1856),_[The Coral Island](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Coral\_Island "The Coral Island")_(1857),_The World of Ice_(1859),_Ungava: a Tale of Eskimo Land_(1857),_The Dog Crusoe_(1860),_The Lighthouse_(1865),_Fighting the Whales_(1866),_Deep Down_(1868),_[The Pirate City](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Pirate\_City:\_An\_Algerine\_Tale "The Pirate City: An Algerine Tale")_(1874),_Erling the Bold_(1869),_The Settler and the Savage_(1877), and more than 100 other books followed in regular succession, his rule being to write as far as possible from personal knowledge of the scenes he described. _[The Gorilla Hunters. _The Coral Island_ is the most popular of the Ballantyne novels still read and remembered today,but because of one mistake he made in that book, in which he gave an incorrect thickness of coconut shells, he subsequently attempted to gain first-hand knowledge of his subject matter. For instance, he spent some time living with the lighthouse keepers at the[Bell Rock](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Rock_Lighthouse "Bell Rock Lighthouse")before writing _The Lighthouse_, and while researching for _Deep Down_ he spent time with the[tin miners](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tin_mining "Tin mining")of[Cornwall](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall "Cornwall").

Hugo was at the forefront of the[Romantic literary movement](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanticism "Romanticism")with his play _[Cromwell](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cromwell\_(play) "Cromwell (play)")_ and drama _[Hernani](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hernani\_(drama) "Hernani (drama)")_. Going by the name **Marie Louise de la Ramée**and known by the[pseudonym](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudonym "Pseudonym")**Ouida**wrote more than 40 novels, as well as short stories, children’s books and essays. Moderately successful, she lived a life of luxury, entertaining many of the literary figures of the day.

_[Under Two Flags](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Under\_Two\_Flags\_(novel))_(1867), one of her most famous novels, described the British in[Algeria](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algeria "Algeria"). It expressed sympathy for the French colonists – with whom Ouida deeply identified – and, to some extent, the[Arabs](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabs "Arabs"). The novel was adapted for the stage, and was filmed six times. Her 1872 novel _[A Dog of Flanders](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Dog\_of\_Flanders "A Dog of Flanders")_ is considered a children’s classic in much of[Asia](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia"). The American author [Jack London](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_London "Jack London")cited her novel _Signa_ as one of the reasons for his literary success. Her lavish lifestyle eventually led her to penury, and her works were put up for auction to pay her debts. She died in Italy from[pneumonia](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pneumonia "Pneumonia"). Soon after her death, her friends organized a public subscription in[Bury St Edmunds](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bury_St_Edmunds "Bury St Edmunds"), her birthplace, where they had a fountain for horses and dogs installed in her name.

[**Henry James**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_James)(American)  
 (April 15, 1843 – February 28,1916)

He was an American-British author. He is regarded as a key transitional figure between [literary realism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_realism "Literary realism")and[literary modernism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_modernism "Literary modernism"), and is considered by many to be among the greatest novelists in the English language. He was the son of[Henry James Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_James_Sr. "Henry James Sr.")and the brother of philosopher and psychologist[William James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_James "William James")and diarist[Alice James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_James "Alice James").

He is best known for his novels dealing with the social and marital interplay between _émigré_ Americans, the English, and continental Europeans, such as _[The Portrait of a Lady](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Portrait\_of\_a\_Lady "The Portrait of a Lady")_. His later works, such as _[The Ambassadors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ambassadors "The Ambassadors")_,_[The Wings of the Dove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Wings\_of\_the\_Dove "The Wings of the Dove")_ and _[The Golden Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Golden\_Bowl "The Golden Bowl")_ were increasingly experimental. In describing the internal states of mind and social dynamics of his characters, James often wrote in a style in which ambiguous or contradictory motives and impressions were overlaid or juxtaposed in the discussion of a character’s psyche. For their unique ambiguity, as well as for other aspects of their composition, his late works have been compared to[Impressionist painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism").

His novella _[The Turn of the Screw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Turn\_of\_the\_Screw "The Turn of the Screw")_ has garnered a reputation as the most analysed and ambiguous[ghost story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghost_story "Ghost story")in the English language and remains his most widely adapted work in other media. He wrote other highly regarded ghost stories, such as “[The Jolly Corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Jolly_Corner "The Jolly Corner")“.

Upon publishing _Twice-Told Tales_, however, he noted, “I do not think much of them,” and he expected little response from the public.[[103]](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathaniel_Hawthorne#cite_note-103)His four major[romances](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novel#19th-century_novels "Novel")were written between 1850 and 1860:_[The Scarlet Letter](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Scarlet\_Letter "The Scarlet Letter")_(1850),_[The House of the Seven Gables](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_House\_of\_the\_Seven\_Gables "The House of the Seven Gables")_(1851),_[The Blithedale Romance](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Blithedale\_Romance "The Blithedale Romance")_(1852) and _[The Marble Faun](https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Marble\_Faun "The Marble Faun")_(1860). Lawrence") ( September 11, 1885 – March 2, 1930) called it a “perfect work of the American imagination”
