**Evangeline Walton** (24 November 1907 – 11 March 1996) was the pen name of **Evangeline Wilna Ensley**, an American writer of fantasy fiction. She remains popular in North America and Europe because of her “ability to humanize historical and mythological subjects with eloquence, humor and compassion”.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-spencer-1)

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evangeline_Walton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

Born in [Indianapolis, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis,_Indiana "Indianapolis, Indiana") to Marion Edmund Ensley and Wilna Eunice Ensley née Coyner, Walton came from a lively, educated, Quaker family. Walton suffered chronic respiratory illnesses as a child, and was privately or self-taught at home. Her parents separated and divorced in 1924. Growing up and living with her mother and her grandmother and witnessing her parents’ marital difficulties roused a natural feminism in Walton which appears throughout her writings. As a child, Walton enjoyed the works of [L. Frank Baum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Frank_Baum "L. Frank Baum"), [James Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Stephens_(author) "James Stephens (author)"), [Lord Dunsany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Dunsany "Lord Dunsany") and [Algernon Blackwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Blackwood "Algernon Blackwood"), which she would later cite as influences on her fiction.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-kies-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-3) Walton and her mother traveled often to New York City, Chicago and San Francisco for opera, especially for [Richard Wagner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wagner "Richard Wagner")’s [Der Ring des Nibelungen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Ring_des_Nibelungen "Der Ring des Nibelungen"); opera was a passion her entire life. In 1946 after the death of her grandmother, Walton and her mother moved to [Tucson, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucson,_Arizona "Tucson, Arizona"). Wilna Ensley died in 1971 but not before she saw the dawn of public recognition for Walton and her works.

Most of Walton’s published and unpublished works were originally written in the 1920s through the early 1950s. She worked on her best known work, the Mabinogion tetralogy, during the late 1930s and early 1940s, and her Theseus trilogy during the late 1940s. Once success found her after 1970, she reworked many of her manuscripts for publication over the next twenty years. Walton said of her knack for writing fantasy: “My own method has always been to try to put flesh and blood on the bones of the original myth; I almost never contradict sources, I only add and interpret.”[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-spencer-1) In 1991, she underwent surgery for a brain tumor that proved benign. However, her health continued to decline.

Treated as a child with [silver nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_nitrate "Silver nitrate") tincture for frequent bronchitis and severe sinus infections, Walton, who had extremely fair skin, absorbed the pigment of the tincture, causing her skin to [turn blue-gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyria "Argyria") and darken as she aged.

Walton corresponded with the British novelist, essayist and poet [John Cowper Powys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cowper_Powys "John Cowper Powys") for many years. Some of Walton's papers from 1936 to 1984—including biographic material, manuscripts and the correspondence with Powys—are archived in Special Collections at the Library, University of Arizona in Tucson. She was first cousin to [Clifford C. Furnas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas "Clifford C. Furnas") (1900–1969), author of _The Next Hundred Years_, Assistant Secretary of War in the Eisenhower administration, co-founder of NASA and chancellor of SUNY Buffalo; and to [Clifton J. Furness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifton_J._Furness?action=edit&redlink=1 "Clifton J. Furness (page does not exist)") (1898–1946), professor of music and author of _The Genteel Female: An Anthology_ (1931). Furness edited and introduced a facsimile edition of _[Leaves of Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaves\_of\_Grass "Leaves of Grass")_ (1939) and _Walt Whitman's Workshop: A Collection of Unpublished Manuscripts_ (1928). A writer himself, Furness encouraged, inspired and mentored his young cousin Evangeline.

Walton herself wrote about her chosen pen name, "I use the name Walton professionally, partly because I originally hoped to build up different lines of work under different names, partly because Walton is an old family name and appears on the Declaration of Independence. Not that I can trace any blood connection between my Quaker Waltons and the Declaration signer. They came from Virginia, and were supposed to have had a [Native American] man somewhere up the family tree. He may be the reason why both records and tradition trail off into vagueness. But when I was a child, old folk remembered the Waltons as very tall, very dark people, too full of restless energy to fit quietly into their peaceful little Quaker community: a vivid, turbulent note in it."

## Writings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evangeline_Walton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writings")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/24/Firsteditioncrop.jpg/250px-Firsteditioncrop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Firsteditioncrop.jpg)

Evangeline Walton with her first edition, 1936

Walton is best known for her four novels retelling the Welsh [Mabinogi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mabinogi "Mabinogi"). She published her first volume in 1936 under the publisher's title of _The Virgin and the Swine_. Although receiving warm praise from [John Cowper Powys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cowper_Powys "John Cowper Powys"), the book sold poorly and none of the other novels in the series reached print at the time. It was rediscovered by [Ballantine's Adult Fantasy series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballantine_Adult_Fantasy_series "Ballantine Adult Fantasy series") in 1970, and reissued as _[The Island of the Mighty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Island\_of\_the\_Mighty "The Island of the Mighty")_.

Editors at Ballantine were unaware that she was still alive, till she got in touch and sent them a second novel that had been left unfinished when the first failed to sell. This appeared as _[The Children of Llyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Children\_of\_Llyr "The Children of Llyr")_ (1971).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-4) It was followed by _[The Song of Rhiannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Song\_of\_Rhiannon "The Song of Rhiannon")_ (1972) and _[Prince of Annwn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince\_of\_Annwn "Prince of Annwn")_ (1974). All four novels were published in a single volume as _The Mabinogion Tetralogy_ (2002) by [Overlook Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overlook_Press "Overlook Press"). The four novels are translated and available in several European languages. The rights to Walton’s Mabinogi work were purchased by [Stevie Nicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Nicks "Stevie Nicks") in the hopes of bringing the epic to the big screen.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-5)

Walton's _[Witch House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witch\_House "Witch House")_ was written in the mid- to late-1930s and published in 1945 as the first volume in “The Library of Arkham House Novels of Fantasy and Terror”. It is an occult horror story set in New England. In 1956, she published _The Cross and the Sword_, a historical novel set during the Danish conquest of England and the destruction of its Celtic culture.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-kies-2)

In 1983, Walton published _[The Sword Is Forged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sword\_Is\_Forged "The Sword Is Forged")_, the first of a planned [Theseus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theseus "Theseus") trilogy.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-kies-2) Walton had completed the trilogy in the late 1940s but the publication by [Mary Renault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Renault "Mary Renault") of her Theseus novels in 1958 and 1962 kept Walton from publishing her own. The remaining two novels in the trilogy remain unpublished.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-6)

Walton published several [short stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_stories "Short stories"). The best-known of these are “Above Ker-Is” (1980), “The Judgement of St.Yves” (1981) and “The Mistress of Kaer-Mor” (1980). She also wrote seven unpublished novels, several volumes of unpublished short stories, poems, and a [verse play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verse_play "Verse play"). Some of these works have been published posthumously: See bibliography below.

[Douglas A. Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_A._Anderson "Douglas A. Anderson") is the agent for Walton's literary works.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Evangeline Walton** (24 November 1907 – 11 March 1996) was the pen name of **Evangeline Wilna Ensley**, an American writer of fantasy fiction. She remains popular in North America and Europe because of her “ability to humanize historical and mythological subjects with eloquence, humor and compassion”.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-spencer-1)

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evangeline_Walton&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

Born in [Indianapolis, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis,_Indiana "Indianapolis, Indiana") to Marion Edmund Ensley and Wilna Eunice Ensley née Coyner, Walton came from a lively, educated, Quaker family. Walton suffered chronic respiratory illnesses as a child, and was privately or self-taught at home. Her parents separated and divorced in 1924. Growing up and living with her mother and her grandmother and witnessing her parents’ marital difficulties roused a natural feminism in Walton which appears throughout her writings. As a child, Walton enjoyed the works of [L. Frank Baum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Frank_Baum "L. Frank Baum"), [James Stephens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Stephens_(author) "James Stephens (author)"), [Lord Dunsany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Dunsany "Lord Dunsany") and [Algernon Blackwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algernon_Blackwood "Algernon Blackwood"), which she would later cite as influences on her fiction.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-kies-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-3) Walton and her mother traveled often to New York City, Chicago and San Francisco for opera, especially for [Richard Wagner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wagner "Richard Wagner")’s [Der Ring des Nibelungen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Der_Ring_des_Nibelungen "Der Ring des Nibelungen"); opera was a passion her entire life. In 1946 after the death of her grandmother, Walton and her mother moved to [Tucson, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucson,_Arizona "Tucson, Arizona"). Wilna Ensley died in 1971 but not before she saw the dawn of public recognition for Walton and her works.

Most of Walton’s published and unpublished works were originally written in the 1920s through the early 1950s. She worked on her best known work, the Mabinogion tetralogy, during the late 1930s and early 1940s, and her Theseus trilogy during the late 1940s. Once success found her after 1970, she reworked many of her manuscripts for publication over the next twenty years. Walton said of her knack for writing fantasy: “My own method has always been to try to put flesh and blood on the bones of the original myth; I almost never contradict sources, I only add and interpret.”[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-spencer-1) In 1991, she underwent surgery for a brain tumor that proved benign. However, her health continued to decline.

Treated as a child with [silver nitrate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_nitrate "Silver nitrate") tincture for frequent bronchitis and severe sinus infections, Walton, who had extremely fair skin, absorbed the pigment of the tincture, causing her skin to [turn blue-gray](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyria "Argyria") and darken as she aged.

Walton corresponded with the British novelist, essayist and poet [John Cowper Powys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cowper_Powys "John Cowper Powys") for many years. Some of Walton's papers from 1936 to 1984—including biographic material, manuscripts and the correspondence with Powys—are archived in Special Collections at the Library, University of Arizona in Tucson. She was first cousin to [Clifford C. Furnas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas "Clifford C. Furnas") (1900–1969), author of _The Next Hundred Years_, Assistant Secretary of War in the Eisenhower administration, co-founder of NASA and chancellor of SUNY Buffalo; and to [Clifton J. Furness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifton_J._Furness?action=edit&redlink=1 "Clifton J. Furness (page does not exist)") (1898–1946), professor of music and author of _The Genteel Female: An Anthology_ (1931). Furness edited and introduced a facsimile edition of _[Leaves of Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaves\_of\_Grass "Leaves of Grass")_ (1939) and _Walt Whitman's Workshop: A Collection of Unpublished Manuscripts_ (1928). A writer himself, Furness encouraged, inspired and mentored his young cousin Evangeline.

Walton herself wrote about her chosen pen name, "I use the name Walton professionally, partly because I originally hoped to build up different lines of work under different names, partly because Walton is an old family name and appears on the Declaration of Independence. Not that I can trace any blood connection between my Quaker Waltons and the Declaration signer. They came from Virginia, and were supposed to have had a [Native American] man somewhere up the family tree. He may be the reason why both records and tradition trail off into vagueness. But when I was a child, old folk remembered the Waltons as very tall, very dark people, too full of restless energy to fit quietly into their peaceful little Quaker community: a vivid, turbulent note in it."

## Writings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Evangeline_Walton&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writings")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/2/24/Firsteditioncrop.jpg/250px-Firsteditioncrop.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Firsteditioncrop.jpg)

Evangeline Walton with her first edition, 1936

Walton is best known for her four novels retelling the Welsh [Mabinogi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mabinogi "Mabinogi"). She published her first volume in 1936 under the publisher's title of _The Virgin and the Swine_. Although receiving warm praise from [John Cowper Powys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cowper_Powys "John Cowper Powys"), the book sold poorly and none of the other novels in the series reached print at the time. It was rediscovered by [Ballantine's Adult Fantasy series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballantine_Adult_Fantasy_series "Ballantine Adult Fantasy series") in 1970, and reissued as _[The Island of the Mighty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Island\_of\_the\_Mighty "The Island of the Mighty")_.

Editors at Ballantine were unaware that she was still alive, till she got in touch and sent them a second novel that had been left unfinished when the first failed to sell. This appeared as _[The Children of Llyr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Children\_of\_Llyr "The Children of Llyr")_ (1971).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-4) It was followed by _[The Song of Rhiannon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Song\_of\_Rhiannon "The Song of Rhiannon")_ (1972) and _[Prince of Annwn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince\_of\_Annwn "Prince of Annwn")_ (1974). All four novels were published in a single volume as _The Mabinogion Tetralogy_ (2002) by [Overlook Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overlook_Press "Overlook Press"). The four novels are translated and available in several European languages. The rights to Walton’s Mabinogi work were purchased by [Stevie Nicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevie_Nicks "Stevie Nicks") in the hopes of bringing the epic to the big screen.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-5)

Walton's _[Witch House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witch\_House "Witch House")_ was written in the mid- to late-1930s and published in 1945 as the first volume in “The Library of Arkham House Novels of Fantasy and Terror”. It is an occult horror story set in New England. In 1956, she published _The Cross and the Sword_, a historical novel set during the Danish conquest of England and the destruction of its Celtic culture.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-kies-2)

In 1983, Walton published _[The Sword Is Forged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sword\_Is\_Forged "The Sword Is Forged")_, the first of a planned [Theseus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theseus "Theseus") trilogy.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-kies-2) Walton had completed the trilogy in the late 1940s but the publication by [Mary Renault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Renault "Mary Renault") of her Theseus novels in 1958 and 1962 kept Walton from publishing her own. The remaining two novels in the trilogy remain unpublished.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evangeline_Walton#cite_note-6)

Walton published several [short stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_stories "Short stories"). The best-known of these are “Above Ker-Is” (1980), “The Judgement of St.Yves” (1981) and “The Mistress of Kaer-Mor” (1980). She also wrote seven unpublished novels, several volumes of unpublished short stories, poems, and a [verse play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verse_play "Verse play"). Some of these works have been published posthumously: See bibliography below.

[Douglas A. Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_A._Anderson "Douglas A. Anderson") is the agent for Walton's literary works.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Clifford Cook Furnas** (October 24, 1900 – April 27, 1969) was an American author, Olympic athlete, scientist, expert on guided missiles, university president, and public servant. He was first cousin of the author Evangeline Walton.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-1) Furnas participated in the [5,000-meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") event at the [1920 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920_Summer_Olympics "1920 Summer Olympics") in [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp"), [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-ann-2)

He taught [chemical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_engineering "Chemical engineering") at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), and directed the airplane division of [Curtiss-Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss-Wright "Curtiss-Wright") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). He became the ninth chancellor of the private [University of Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Buffalo "University of Buffalo") in 1954.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-Bio-3) After guiding the University through the merger process with the [State University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York "State University of New York") in 1962, Furnas became the first president of the [State University of New York at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York_at_Buffalo "State University of New York at Buffalo").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-ann-2) Between 1955 and 1957 he was on a leave of absence to serve as Assistant Secretary of Defense during the [Eisenhower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower "Dwight D. Eisenhower") administration.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-Bio-3)

He retired from the University of Buffalo in 1966 and died in 1969 at age 68.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-Bio-3)

**Clifford Cook Furnas** (October 24, 1900 – April 27, 1969) was an American author, Olympic athlete, scientist, expert on guided missiles, university president, and public servant. He was first cousin of the author Evangeline Walton.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-1) Furnas participated in the [5,000-meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") event at the [1920 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920_Summer_Olympics "1920 Summer Olympics") in [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp"), [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-ann-2)

He taught [chemical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_engineering "Chemical engineering") at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), and directed the airplane division of [Curtiss-Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss-Wright "Curtiss-Wright") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). He became the ninth chancellor of the private [University of Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Buffalo "University of Buffalo") in 1954.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-Bio-3) After guiding the University through the merger process with the [State University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York "State University of New York") in 1962, Furnas became the first president of the [State University of New York at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York_at_Buffalo "State University of New York at Buffalo").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-ann-2) Between 1955 and 1957 he was on a leave of absence to serve as Assistant Secretary of Defense during the [Eisenhower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower "Dwight D. Eisenhower") administration.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-Bio-3)

He retired from the University of Buffalo in 1966 and died in 1969 at age 68.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-Bio-3)

## Education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_Furnas&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education")]

*   1922 B.S., with honors, [Purdue University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purdue_University "Purdue University")
*   1926 Ph.D., [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan")
*   1946 [Honorary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_degree "Honorary degree") Doctor of Engineering, [Purdue University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purdue_University "Purdue University")
*   1957 Honorary Doctor of Engineering, [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan")

*   1960 Honorary Doctor of Science, [Thiel College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiel_College "Thiel College")
*   1963 Degree Honoris Causa, [Universidad Nacional de Asunción](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_Nacional_de_Asunci%C3%B3n "Universidad Nacional de Asunción") of [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay")

## Academic career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_Furnas&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Academic career")]

*   1922–1924 Math teacher, [Shattuck School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shattuck-Saint_Mary's "Shattuck-Saint Mary's"), [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota")
*   1924–1925 Research Chemist, [U.S. Steel Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Steel_Corporation "U.S. Steel Corporation")
*   1926–1931 Physical Chemist, [U.S. Bureau of Mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Bureau_of_Mines "U.S. Bureau of Mines")
*   1931–1941 Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering, [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")
*   1941–1942 Technical aide at the [National Defense Research Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Defense_Research_Committee "National Defense Research Committee")
*   1943–1946 Director of Curtiss-Wright Aeronautical Research Laboratory in [Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York"), New York
*   1946–1954 Director and Executive Vice President, [Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calspan "Calspan")
*   1954–1962 [Chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)"), University at Buffalo
*   1962–1966 President, [State University of New York at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo,_The_State_University_of_New_York "University at Buffalo, The State University of New York")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clifford_C._Furnas#cite_note-University_at_Buffalo-5)
*   1962–1966 President, Western New York Nuclear Research
*   1966–1969 President Emeritus, [State University of New York at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo,_The_State_University_of_New_York "University at Buffalo, The State University of New York")

## Government career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_Furnas&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Government career")]

*   1952–1953 Chairman, Guided Missile Commission, Research and Development Board
*   1954–1957 Chairman, [U.S. Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Department_of_Defense "U.S. Department of Defense") Advisory Panel on Aeronautics
*   1954–1969 Member, [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army "U.S. Army") Science Advisory Panel
*   1955–1957 Member of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics
*   1955–1957 Assistant Secretary of Defense for Research and Development
*   1956–1957 Chairman, Air Navigation Development Board
*   1957–1969 Member of the [Defense Science Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Science_Board "Defense Science Board")
*   1958–1969 Member of the [Naval Research Advisory Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Research_Advisory_Committee "Naval Research Advisory Committee")
*   1961–1965 Chairman of the Defense Science Board
*   1961–1969 Chairman, New York Advisory Council, Industrial Research and Development
*   1968–1969 Vice-Chairman, [National Research Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Research_Council_(United_States) "National Research Council (United States)")

**Clifford Cook Furnas** (October 24, 1900 – April 27, 1969) was an American author, Olympic athlete, scientist, expert on guided missiles, university president, and public servant. He was first cousin of the author Evangeline Walton.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-1) Furnas participated in the [5,000-meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") event at the [1920 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920_Summer_Olympics "1920 Summer Olympics") in [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp"), [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-ann-2)

He taught [chemical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_engineering "Chemical engineering") at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), and directed the airplane division of [Curtiss-Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss-Wright "Curtiss-Wright") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). He became the ninth chancellor of the private [University of Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Buffalo "University of Buffalo") in 1954.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-Bio-3) After guiding the University through the merger process with the [State University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York "State University of New York") in 1962, Furnas became the first president of the [State University of New York at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York_at_Buffalo "State University of New York at Buffalo").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-ann-2) Between 1955 and 1957 he was on a leave of absence to serve as Assistant Secretary of Defense during the [Eisenhower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower "Dwight D. Eisenhower") administration.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-Bio-3)

He retired from the University of Buffalo in 1966 and died in 1969 at age 68.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-Bio-3)

## Athletic career

*   1920 Olympic Games, [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp"), [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium")[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-Sports_Reference/Olympic_Sports-4)
*   1922 [Big Ten Conference Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Ten_Medal_of_Honor "Big Ten Medal of Honor"), for best combined scholastic and athletic record

## Education

*   1922 B.S., with honors, [Purdue University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purdue_University "Purdue University")
*   1926 Ph.D., [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan")
*   1946 [Honorary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_degree "Honorary degree") Doctor of Engineering, [Purdue University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purdue_University "Purdue University")
*   1957 Honorary Doctor of Engineering, [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan")
*   1958 Honorary Doctor of Laws, [Alfred University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_University "Alfred University")
*   1960 Honorary Doctor of Science, [Thiel College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiel_College "Thiel College")
*   1963 Degree Honoris Causa, [Universidad Nacional de Asunción](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universidad_Nacional_de_Asunci%C3%B3n "Universidad Nacional de Asunción") of [Paraguay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paraguay "Paraguay")

## Academic career

*   1922–1924 Math teacher, [Shattuck School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shattuck-Saint_Mary's "Shattuck-Saint Mary's"), [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota")
*   1924–1925 Research Chemist, [U.S. Steel Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Steel_Corporation "U.S. Steel Corporation")
*   1926–1931 Physical Chemist, [U.S. Bureau of Mines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Bureau_of_Mines "U.S. Bureau of Mines")
*   1931–1941 Associate Professor of Chemical Engineering, [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University")
*   1941–1942 Technical aide at the [National Defense Research Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Defense_Research_Committee "National Defense Research Committee")
*   1943–1946 Director of Curtiss-Wright Aeronautical Research Laboratory in [Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffalo,_New_York "Buffalo, New York"), New York
*   1946–1954 Director and Executive Vice President, [Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calspan "Calspan")
*   1954–1962 [Chancellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chancellor_(education) "Chancellor (education)"), University at Buffalo
*   1962–1966 President, [State University of New York at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo,_The_State_University_of_New_York "University at Buffalo, The State University of New York")[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-University_at_Buffalo-5)
*   1962–1966 President, Western New York Nuclear Research
*   1966–1969 President Emeritus, [State University of New York at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_at_Buffalo,_The_State_University_of_New_York "University at Buffalo, The State University of New York")

## Government career

*   1952–1953 Chairman, Guided Missile Commission, Research and Development Board
*   1954–1957 Chairman, [U.S. Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Department_of_Defense "U.S. Department of Defense") Advisory Panel on Aeronautics
*   1954–1969 Member, [U.S. Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army "U.S. Army") Science Advisory Panel
*   1955–1957 Member of the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics
*   1955–1957 Assistant Secretary of Defense for Research and Development
*   1956–1957 Chairman, Air Navigation Development Board
*   1957–1969 Member of the [Defense Science Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Science_Board "Defense Science Board")
*   1958–1969 Member of the [Naval Research Advisory Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval_Research_Advisory_Committee "Naval Research Advisory Committee")
*   1961–1965 Chairman of the Defense Science Board
*   1961–1969 Chairman, New York Advisory Council, Industrial Research and Development
*   1968–1969 Vice-Chairman, [National Research Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Research_Council_(United_States) "National Research Council (United States)")

**Clifford Cook Furnas** (October 24, 1900 – April 27, 1969) was an American author, Olympic athlete, scientist, expert on guided missiles, university president, and public servant. He was first cousin of the author Evangeline Walton.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-1) Furnas participated in the [5,000-meter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") event at the [1920 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920_Summer_Olympics "1920 Summer Olympics") in [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp"), [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-ann-2)

He taught [chemical engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chemical_engineering "Chemical engineering") at [Yale University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), and directed the airplane division of [Curtiss-Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtiss-Wright "Curtiss-Wright") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). He became the ninth chancellor of the private [University of Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Buffalo "University of Buffalo") in 1954.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-Bio-3) After guiding the University through the merger process with the [State University of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York "State University of New York") in 1962, Furnas became the first president of the [State University of New York at Buffalo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York_at_Buffalo "State University of New York at Buffalo").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-ann-2) Between 1955 and 1957 he was on a leave of absence to serve as Assistant Secretary of Defense during the [Eisenhower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_D._Eisenhower "Dwight D. Eisenhower") administration.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-Bio-3)

He retired from the University of Buffalo in 1966 and died in 1969 at age 68.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Clifford_C._Furnas&printable=yes#cite_note-Bio-3)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [List of tornadoes and tornado outbreaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_tornadoes_and_tornado_outbreaks&redirect=no "List of tornadoes and tornado outbreaks"))

These are some notable [tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado"), [tornado outbreaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak"), and [tornado outbreak sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence "Tornado outbreak sequence") that have occurred around the globe.

1.   _Exact death and injury counts are not possible; especially for large events and events before 1955._
2.   _Prior to 1950 in the United States, only significant tornadoes are listed for the number of tornadoes in outbreaks._
3.   _Due to increasing detection, particularly in the U.S., numbers of counted tornadoes have increased markedly in recent decades although the number of actual tornadoes and counted [significant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary\_of\_tornado\_terms#S "Glossary of tornado terms") tornadoes has not. In older events, the number of tornadoes officially counted is likely underestimated._

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

(Redirected from [List of tornadoes and tornado outbreaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_tornadoes_and_tornado_outbreaks&redirect=no "List of tornadoes and tornado outbreaks"))

These are some notable [tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado"), [tornado outbreaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak"), and [tornado outbreak sequences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_sequence "Tornado outbreak sequence") that have occurred around the globe.

1.   _Exact death and injury counts are not possible; especially for large events and events before 1955._
2.   _Prior to 1950 in the United States, only significant tornadoes are listed for the number of tornadoes in outbreaks._
3.   _Due to increasing detection, particularly in the U.S., numbers of counted tornadoes have increased markedly in recent decades although the number of actual tornadoes and counted [significant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary\_of\_tornado\_terms#S "Glossary of tornado terms") tornadoes has not. In older events, the number of tornadoes officially counted is likely underestimated._

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

List of world records related to tornadoes

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Super_Outbreak_Map.jpg/250px-Super_Outbreak_Map.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Super_Outbreak_Map.jpg)

A map of the tornado paths in the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak")

This article lists various **tornado records**. The most "extreme" [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") in recorded history was the [Tri-State tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1925_Tri-State_tornado "1925 Tri-State tornado"), which spread through parts of [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), and [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") on March 18, 1925. It was likely an F5 on the [Fujita Scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_Scale "Fujita Scale") (tornadoes were not rated at the time) and holds records for longest path length at 219 miles (352 km) and longest duration at about 3+1⁄2 hours. The 2014 [Pilger, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilger,_Nebraska "Pilger, Nebraska") tornado had the highest forward speed ever recorded in a violent tornado, at 94 mph (151 km/h). The deadliest tornado in world history was the [Daulatpur–Saturia tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daulatpur%E2%80%93Saturia_tornado "Daulatpur–Saturia tornado") in Bangladesh on April 26, 1989, which killed approximately 1,300 people.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Bangladesh_tornado-1) In the history of Bangladesh, at least 24 tornadoes killed more than 100 people each, almost half of the total for the world.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-2) The most extensive [tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak") on record was the [2011 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak "2011 Super Outbreak"), which resulted in 367 tornadoes and 324 tornadic fatalities,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-super_outbreak-3) whereas the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak") was the [most intense tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tornado_outbreaks_by_outbreak_intensity_score "List of tornado outbreaks by outbreak intensity score") on tornado expert [Thomas P. Grazulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis "Thomas P. Grazulis")'s [outbreak intensity score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis#Outbreak_intensity_score "Thomas P. Grazulis") with 578, as opposed to the 2011 outbreak's 378.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-4) The widest tornado recorded was the [2013 El Reno tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_El_Reno_tornado "2013 El Reno tornado"), having a width of 2.6 miles (4.2 km), and killing eight people including veteran storm chaser [Tim Samaras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Samaras "Tim Samaras").

The 2011 Super Outbreak was the largest tornado outbreak spawned by a single weather system in recorded history; it produced 367 tornadoes from April 25–28, with 223 of those in a single 24-hour period on April 27 from midnight to midnight [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-2011NCDC-5)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-tornado-largest-tornado-outbreak-12) fifteen of which were violent EF4–EF5 tornadoes. 348 deaths occurred in that outbreak, of which 324 were tornado-related. The outbreak largely contributed to the record for most tornadoes in April with [780 tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_tornadoes_in_April_2011 "List of United States tornadoes in April 2011"), almost triple the prior record (267 in April 1974). The overall record for a single month was 542 in May 2003, which was also broken.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-April_2011_tornado_information-13)

The 1974 Super Outbreak of April 3–4, which spawned 148 confirmed tornadoes across eastern North America, held the record for the most prolific tornado outbreak in terms of overall tornadoes for many years, and as of October 2025, it still holds the record for most violent, long-track tornadoes (7 F5 and 23 F4 tornadoes). More significant tornadoes occurred within 24 hours than any other day on record.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-1974NCDC-6)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-tornado_outbreak_sequences-14) Due to advancements in technology allowing for more accuracy in tornado reporting, the 2011 and 1974 tornado counts are not directly comparable.

### Longest continuous outbreak and largest autumnal outbreak

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Longest continuous outbreak and largest autumnal outbreak")]

Most tornado outbreaks in North America occur in the spring, but there is a secondary peak of tornado activity in the fall. It is historically less consistent from year to year but can include exceptionally large or intense outbreaks. In 1992, an estimated [95 tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_1992_tornado_outbreak "November 1992 tornado outbreak") broke out in a record 41 hours of continuous [tornado activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_1992_tornado_outbreak "November 1992 tornado outbreak") from November 21 to 23. This is also among the largest-known outbreaks in areal expanse. Many other very large outbreaks have occurred in autumn, especially in October and November, such as the [2002 Veterans Day weekend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_November_9%E2%80%9311,_2002 "Tornado outbreak of November 9–11, 2002") outbreak, in which 83 tornadoes occurred from November 9 to 11, and [November 17, 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_November_17,_2013 "Tornado outbreak of November 17, 2013"), when 73 tornadoes were produced in 11 hours.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Significant_Tornadoes-17)

### Greatest number of tornadoes spawned from a hurricane

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Greatest number of tornadoes spawned from a hurricane")]

The greatest number of tornadoes spawned from a hurricane is 120 from [Hurricane Ivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ivan_tornado_outbreak "Hurricane Ivan tornado outbreak") in September 2004, followed by [Hurricane Beulah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Beulah "Hurricane Beulah") with 115 in September 1967, and 103 from [Hurricane Frances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Frances_tornado_outbreak "Hurricane Frances tornado outbreak") in September 2004 (a couple weeks before Ivan).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-18) Hurricanes prior to the 1990s, when tornado records were more sparse, perhaps produced more tornadoes than were officially documented.

### Most tornadoes in a single year

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Most tornadoes in a single year")]

On average, 1,200 tornadoes happen in a year in the United States. The most confirmed tornadoes in a single year was in [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadoes_of_2004 "Tornadoes of 2004"),[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-26) which had 1817 confirmed tornadoes. This was mostly boosted by a large tornado outbreak sequence in May 2004, where 509 tornadoes occurred. It also had help from a very active fall and winter tornado season.

## Tornado casualties and damage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tornado casualties and damage")]

### Deadliest single tornado in world history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Deadliest single tornado in world history")]

Officially, the deadliest single tornado occurred on April 26, 1989, in Bangladesh, where a [large tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daulatpur%E2%80%93Saturia_tornado "Daulatpur–Saturia tornado") took at least 1,300 lives.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-27) In 2022, this tornado's death toll was challenged in a database of Bangladeshi tornadoes maintained by Dr. Fahim Sufi with the [Australian Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Government "Australian Government"), claiming that the April 14, 1969, [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka") tornado, which killed 922 people, was the deadliest in Bangladesh, with the Jamalpur tornado killing only 570.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-2023_Sustainability-28)

### Deadliest single tornado in US history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Deadliest single tornado in US history")]

The [Tri-State tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1925_Tri-State_tornado "1925 Tri-State tornado") of March 18, 1925, killed 695 people in Missouri (11), Illinois (613), and Indiana (71). The outbreak it occurred with was also the deadliest known tornado outbreak, with a combined death toll of 747 across the [Mississippi River Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River_Valley "Mississippi River Valley").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-NOAA/NWS_1925_Tri-State_Tornado_Statistics-29)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Tri-State_Tornado_Facts-30)

### Most intense tornado damage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Most intense tornado damage")]

The original [Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale "Fujita scale"), developed by [Ted Fujita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Fujita "Ted Fujita"), has never been used to assign a final rating over F5 intensity;[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-32) however, two tornadoes, the [1970 Lubbock tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Lubbock_tornado "1970 Lubbock tornado") and [1974 Xenia tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Xenia_tornado "1974 Xenia tornado"), were initially given F6 ratings by Fujita himself, but both were eventually downgraded to F5 ratings.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-33)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-34) The [1976 Jordan tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Jordan_tornado "1976 Jordan tornado") was described by Fujita as the most intense tornado damage he had surveyed up to that point.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-35)

A more recent example of extreme damage was at the Double Creek Estates of [Jarrell, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarrell,_Texas "Jarrell, Texas"); the [1997 Jarrell tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Jarrell_tornado "1997 Jarrell tornado") stalled over the area at peak F5 intensity, destroying every home in the subdivision, and killing 27. Extreme ground scouring and high-end F5 damage was surveyed.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-36) The [2008 Parkersburg tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Parkersburg_tornado "2008 Parkersburg tornado") was reported by mayor Bob Haylock to have been so intense that a majority of the fatalities out of [Parkersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkersburg,_Iowa "Parkersburg, Iowa") were from people taking shelter in basements underground.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-37) The [2011 Philadelphia, Mississippi tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Philadelphia,_Mississippi_tornado "2011 Philadelphia, Mississippi tornado") caused extreme ground scouring across its path; up to .5 m (1.6 ft) of soil was removed from the environment, presumably from intense [subvortices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-vortex_tornado "Multi-vortex tornado").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-BAMS-38)

### Most damaging tornado

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Most damaging tornado")]

The [1896 St. Louis–East St. Louis tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896_St._Louis%E2%80%93East_St._Louis_tornado "1896 St. Louis–East St. Louis tornado") on May 27, incurred the most damages adjusted for inflation, with an estimated $5.36 billion (2022 USD). In raw numbers, the [Joplin tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Joplin_tornado "2011 Joplin tornado") of May 22, 2011, is considered the costliest tornado in recent history, with damage totals at $3.71 billion (2022 USD). Until April 2011, the [Bridge Creek–Moore tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Bridge_Creek-Moore_tornado "1999 Bridge Creek-Moore tornado") of May 3, 1999, was the most costly, which was later surpassed by the [2011 Tuscaloosa–Birmingham tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Tuscaloosa%E2%80%93Birmingham_tornado "2011 Tuscaloosa–Birmingham tornado"), with a damage total of $3.18 billion (2022 USD).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-tornado_damage_normalization-39)

During the F5 [1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Bridge_Creek%E2%80%93Moore_tornado "1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado") on May 3, 1999, in the southern [Oklahoma City metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_Metropolitan_Area "Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area") area, a [Doppler on Wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doppler_on_Wheels "Doppler on Wheels") situated near the tornado measured winds of 301±20 mph (484±32 km/h) momentarily in a small area inside the funnel approximately 100 m (330 ft) above ground level.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-57) The measured winds in this tornado have been updated to 321 miles per hour (517 km/h).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Dow2024-40)

On May 31, 2013, a tornado hit rural areas near [El Reno, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Reno,_Oklahoma "El Reno, Oklahoma"). The tornado was originally rated as an EF3 based on damage; however, after mobile radar data analysis was conducted, it was concluded to have been an EF5 due to a measured wind speed of greater than 296 mph (476 km/h), second only to the Bridge Creek–Moore tornado. Revised RaXPol analysis found winds of 302±34 mph (486±55 km/h) well above ground level and ≥291 mph (468 km/h) below 10 m (33 ft) with some subvortices moving at 175 mph (282 km/h).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-RaXPol-58) These winds may possibly be as high or higher than the winds recorded on May 3, 1999. Despite the recorded windspeed, the El Reno tornado was later downgraded back to EF3 due to the fact that no EF5 damage was found, likely due to the lack of sufficient damage indicators in the largely-rural area west of [Oklahoma City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City "Oklahoma City").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-59)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-60)

During the [Greenfield, Iowa EF4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Greenfield_tornado "2024 Greenfield tornado") on May 21, 2024, [Doppler on Wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doppler_on_Wheels "Doppler on Wheels") recorded wind speeds of 263–271 mph (423–436 km/h) in a very small swath inside the funnel approximately 100–106 ft (30–32 m) above radar level as the tornado went through town. After doing some mathematical and physics-based calculations, the researchers determined those measured winds were equivalent to 309–318 mph (497–512 km/h). The calculated minimum wind threshold as stated beats both the [1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Bridge_Creek%E2%80%93Moore_tornado "1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado") and the [2013 El Reno, Oklahoma tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_El_Reno_tornado "2013 El Reno tornado") for minimum possible maximum windspeed; however, the highest confirmed peak windspeeds are lower than the 1999 tornado.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Wurman-2024-61)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-:3-62)

Winds were measured at 262–280 mph (422–451 km/h) using portable [Doppler weather radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_radar#Velocity "Weather radar") in the [Red Rock, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Rock,_Oklahoma "Red Rock, Oklahoma"), tornado during the [April 26, 1991, tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_26,_1991_tornado_outbreak "April 26, 1991 tornado outbreak") in north-central Oklahoma. Though these winds are possibly indicative of F5 intensity, this particular tornado's path never encountered any significant structures and caused minimal damage, so it was rated F4.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Doppler_Spectra-51)
