### Longest damage path and duration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Longest damage path and duration")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Radar_collage_of_a_long-lived_supercell_radar_on_December_10-11%2C_2021.png/250px-Radar_collage_of_a_long-lived_supercell_radar_on_December_10-11%2C_2021.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Radar_collage_of_a_long-lived_supercell_radar_on_December_10-11,_2021.png)

Radar collage of the [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") that spawned the record-breaking [tornado family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_family "Tornado family") on December 10–11, 2021

The longest-known track for a single tornado is the [Tri-State tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1925_Tri-State_tornado "1925 Tri-State tornado"), occurring on March 18, 1925, with a path length of 151 to 235 mi (243 to 378 km). For years there was debate whether the originally-recognized path length of 219 mi (352 km) over 3.5 hours was from one tornado or a series. Some very long track (VLT) tornadoes were later determined to be successive tornadoes spawned by the same supercell thunderstorm, which are known as a [tornado family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_family "Tornado family"). The Tri-State tornado, however, appeared to have no gaps in the damage. A six-year reanalysis study by a team of severe convective storm meteorologists found insufficient evidence to make firm conclusions but does conclude that it is likely that the beginning and ending of the path was resultant of separate tornadoes comprising a tornado family. It also found that the tornado began 15 mi (24 km) to the west and ended 1 mi (1.6 km) farther east than previously known, bringing the total path to 235 mi (378 km).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The 174 mi (280 km) segment from central [Madison County, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_County,_Missouri "Madison County, Missouri"), to [Pike County, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_County,_Indiana "Pike County, Indiana"), is likely one continuous tornado, and the 151 mi (243 km) segment from central [Bollinger County, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bollinger_County,_Missouri "Bollinger County, Missouri"), to western Pike County, Indiana, is very likely a single continuous tornado. Another [significant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_tornado_terms#S "Glossary of tornado terms") tornado was found about 65 mi (105 km) east-northeast of the end of aforementioned segment(s) of the Tri-State tornado family and is likely another member of the family. Its path length of 20 mi (32 km) over about 20 minutes makes the known tornado family path length total to 320 mi (510 km) over about 5+1⁄2 hours.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Johns-73)[Grazulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis "Thomas P. Grazulis") in 2001 wrote that the first 60 mi (97 km) of the (originally recognized) track is probably the result of two or more tornadoes and that a path length of 157 mi (253 km) was seemingly continuous.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Grazulis2001a-52)

The [2021 Western Kentucky tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado "2021 Western Kentucky tornado") on December 10, 2021, is the longest confirmed track of a tornado.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-74) This violent tornado tracked 165.7 mi (266.7 km) through the states of [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") and [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky") during a [very intense late-season outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021 "Tornado outbreak of December 10–11, 2021"). The tornado was spawned by a very long-tracked [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") that previously dropped [another violent tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Tri-State_tornado "2021 Tri-State tornado") in [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") and [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"), and initial media reports referred to the entire event as the "Quad-state Tornado", which would have had a path of 230 mi (370 km).[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-75)

On March 22, 1953, a tornado touched down near [Leesville, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leesville,_Louisiana "Leesville, Louisiana") at 21:00 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC "UTC"); the tornado continued into far-northwest [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), before dissipating north of [Leland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leland,_Mississippi "Leland, Mississippi"), killing two and injuring 22. The tornado was rated F2 on the [Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale "Fujita scale"). It traveled for 234.7 mi (377.7 km), making it possibly the longest tracked tornado in history, though it is likely that the path consisted of multiple different tornadoes as part of a [tornado family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_family "Tornado family").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-76)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-77)

### Longest path and duration tornado family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Longest path and duration tornado family")]

What at one time was thought to be the record holder for the longest tornado path is now thought to be the longest tornado family, with a track of at least 293 miles (472 km) on May 26, 1917, from the Missouri border across Illinois into Indiana. It caused severe damage and mass casualties in [Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_Illinois "Charleston, Illinois") and [Mattoon, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattoon,_Illinois "Mattoon, Illinois").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Significant_Tornadoes-17)

What was probably the longest track [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") thunderstorm tracked 790 miles (1,270 km) across 6 states in 17.5 hours on March 12, 2006, as part of the [March 2006 tornado outbreak sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_2006_tornado_outbreak_sequence "March 2006 tornado outbreak sequence"). It began in [Noble County, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_County,_Oklahoma "Noble County, Oklahoma"), and ended in [Jackson County, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Michigan "Jackson County, Michigan"), producing many tornadoes in Missouri and Illinois.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-six_state_supercell-78)

### Largest path width

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Largest path width")]

Main article: [List of tornadoes by width](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tornadoes_by_width "List of tornadoes by width")

Officially, the widest tornado on record is the [El Reno, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Reno,_Oklahoma "El Reno, Oklahoma")[tornado of May 31, 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_El_Reno_tornado "2013 El Reno tornado"), with a width of 2.6 miles (4.2 km) at its peak. This is the width found by the National Weather Service based on preliminary data from University of Oklahoma RaXPol mobile radar that also sampled winds of 296 mph (476 km/h), which was used to upgrade the tornado to EF5.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-79) However, it was revealed that these winds did not impact any structures, and as a result the tornado was downgraded to EF3 based on damage.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-80)

The F4 [Hallam, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallam,_Nebraska "Hallam, Nebraska"), [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Hallam_tornado "2004 Hallam tornado") during the [outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_2004_tornado_outbreak_sequence "May 2004 tornado outbreak sequence") of May 22, 2004, was the previous official record holder for the widest tornado, surveyed at 2.5 miles (4.0 km) wide. A similar size tornado struck [Edmonson, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonson,_Texas "Edmonson, Texas") on May 31, 1968, when a damage path width between 2 and 3 miles (3.2 and 4.8 km) was recorded from an F3 tornado.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-81) Another tornado with a similar width struck [Maxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxton,_North_Carolina "Maxton, North Carolina") and [Red Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Springs,_North_Carolina "Red Springs, North Carolina") during the [March 28, 1984, Carolina Tornado Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Carolinas_tornado_outbreak "1984 Carolinas tornado outbreak"); this tornado had a width of 2.5 miles wide at one point. Rated as F4, the tornado resulted in 3 fatalities and 280 injuries.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-82) The EF4 [Jiangsu tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiangsu_tornado "Jiangsu tornado") on June 23, 2016, also had a peak width of 4.1 km wide (2.55 miles).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-83)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-twister.caps.ou.edu-84)

On May 3, 1999, a Doppler On Wheels (DOW) mobile radar observed an F4 tornado as it crossed Mulhall during the [1999 Oklahoma Tornado Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Oklahoma_Tornado_Outbreak "1999 Oklahoma Tornado Outbreak"), which also produced the [Bridge Creek–Moore tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Bridge_Creek-Moore_tornado "1999 Bridge Creek-Moore tornado"). The DOW documented the largest-ever-observed core flow circulation with a distance of 1,600 m (5,200 ft) between peak velocities on either side of the tornado, and a roughly 7 km (4.3 mi) width of peak wind gusts exceeding 43 m/s (96 mph), making the Mulhall tornado the largest tornado ever measured quantitatively.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-FARM-44)

On April 21, 1946, a [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_tornadoes_in_1946#April_21_event "List of United States tornadoes in 1946") struck the area in and around [Timber Lake, South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timber_Lake,_South_Dakota "Timber Lake, South Dakota"). The [U.S. Weather Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") published a paper in 1946 stating the width of this tornado was 4 miles (6.4 km), which would make this the widest tornado ever documented in history. However, this is outside the period of reliable documentation accepted by the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service"), which is 1950–present.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-April_MWR-85)

On [May 19, 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_May_19%E2%80%9322,_2024 "Tornado outbreak of May 19–22, 2024"), a large [multiple-vortex tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple-vortex_tornado "Multiple-vortex tornado") tracked 15 mi (24 km) over rural areas near [Custer City, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custer_City,_Oklahoma "Custer City, Oklahoma"). While the tornado is believed to only have been about 1 mile wide, the maximum width of its tornadic windfield and accompanying damage was nearly 3 mi (4.8 km), making it one of the largest recorded damage paths of any tornado.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-86)

### Smallest and shortest-lived damaging tornado

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Smallest and shortest-lived damaging tornado")]

The smallest and shortest-lived tornado on record to produce surveyable damage was an EF1 tornado on the western side of [Broken Bow, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broken_Bow,_Nebraska "Broken Bow, Nebraska") on July 16, 2024. Spawned from an [outflow-driven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outflow_(meteorology) "Outflow (meteorology)") supercell, a very brief tornado, seen by a chaser and a [surveillance camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveillance_camera "Surveillance camera"), was recorded on the ground for only two seconds, having a listed maximum width of only 1 yard (0.91 m) and a listed path length of 0.01 miles (16 m). Despite this, it was powerful enough to lift and throw a 800 lb (360 kg) trailer into a nearby parked car.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-87)

### Highest forward speed

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Highest forward speed")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Pilger%2C_NE_tornadoes.jpg/250px-Pilger%2C_NE_tornadoes.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pilger,_NE_tornadoes.jpg)

Twin EF4 tornadoes in [Pilger, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilger,_Nebraska "Pilger, Nebraska") on June 16, 2014. The leftmost tornado would achieve the highest forward speed in history.

The highest accepted forward [speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed "Speed") of an intense tornado on record was 75 mph (121 km/h) from the [1974 Guin tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Guin_tornado "1974 Guin tornado") that tore across northwestern Alabama. Other weak tornadoes have approached or exceeded this speed, but this is the fastest forward movement observed in a major tornado.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Significant_Tornadoes-17) The [1977 Birmingham tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_April_1977#Birmingham%E2%80%93Smithfield,_Alabama "Tornado outbreak of April 1977") had an average forward speed of 60 mph (97 km/h),[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-88) as did the [2021 Western Kentucky tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado "2021 Western Kentucky tornado").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-89)

Weaker tornadoes and tornado vortices have been recorded exceeding these speeds. Subvortices of the [2013 El Reno tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_El_Reno_tornado "2013 El Reno tornado") were recorded to travel at speeds of 175 mph (282 km/h) as they orbited the main vortex; the fastest speed a separate tornado-producing mesocyclone has been recorded to travel at was determined via [photogrammetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photogrammetry "Photogrammetry") to be the junior EF4 of the [2014 Pilger, Nebraska, tornado family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Pilger,_Nebraska,_tornado_family "2014 Pilger, Nebraska, tornado family"), travelling at 94.6 mph (152.2 km/h) for five seconds near the very end of its lifespan.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-90) These figures have not been acknowledged by the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service").

Calculations of highest speeds from the [National Centers for Environmental Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Centers_for_Environmental_Information "National Centers for Environmental Information") Storm Events Database gives a high [average forward speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Average_speed "Average speed") of a significant tornado just west of [Galt, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galt,_Iowa "Galt, Iowa"), on December 15, 2021, of between 70.91 mph (114.12 km/h) and 88.65 mph (142.67 km/h).[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-91) This tornado occurred during the [December 2021 Midwest derecho and tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/December_2021_Midwest_derecho_and_tornado_outbreak "December 2021 Midwest derecho and tornado outbreak"), and was accompanied by straight-line winds approaching 80 mph (130 km/h). A faster range can be calculated on an EF1 tornado south of [Taylorville, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylorville,_Illinois "Taylorville, Illinois") on [March 31, 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tornadoes_in_the_tornado_outbreak_of_March_31_%E2%80%93_April_1,_2023#Illinois_(March_31) "List of tornadoes in the tornado outbreak of March 31 – April 1, 2023"), which traveled 1.74 mi (2.80 km) between 18:13 and 18:14, giving a range of forward speeds between 52.2 mph (84.0 km/h) and 104.4 mph (168.0 km/h).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-92) Due to significant variability caused by the unspecific nature of the timestamps provided, these speed figures are unofficial.

### Greatest pressure drop

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Greatest pressure drop")]

A [pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure "Atmospheric pressure") deficit of 100 millibars (2.95 inHg) was observed during a violent [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Manchester_tornado "2003 Manchester tornado") near [Manchester, South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester,_South_Dakota "Manchester, South Dakota") on June 24, 2003, passed directly over an [in-situ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-situ "In-situ") probe deployed by storm chasing researcher [Tim Samaras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Samaras "Tim Samaras").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Manchester-93) In less than a minute, the pressure plunged to 850 millibars (25.10 inHg) at ground level, widely regarded as the lowest reliably measured pressure inside a tornado and, when adjusted to sea level, comparable to the lowest pressures ever recorded in the United States.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-94)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Cerveny-95)

On April 21, 2007, a 194-millibar (5.73 inHg) pressure deficit was reported when a [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_late-April_2007_tornado_outbreak_sequence_tornadoes "List of late-April 2007 tornado outbreak sequence tornadoes") struck a [storm chasing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_chasing "Storm chasing") vehicle in [Tulia, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulia,_Texas "Tulia, Texas").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Tulia-96) The tornado caused EF2 damage as it passed through Tulia. The reported pressure drop far exceeds that which would be expected based on theoretical calculations.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-JAS3489-97)

There is a questionable and unofficial citizen's barometer measurement of a 192-millibar (5.67 inHg) drop around [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") in 1904.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-in-situ_history-98)

## Early tornadoes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Early tornadoes")]

### Earliest-known tornado in Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Earliest-known tornado in Europe")]

*   The earliest recorded tornado in Europe struck [Freising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freising "Freising") (Germany) in 788.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-99)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-100)
*   The earliest-known Irish tornado appeared on April 30, 1054, in Rostella, near [Kilbeggan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilbeggan "Kilbeggan"). The earliest-known British tornado hit central London on October 23, 1091, and was [especially destructive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_tornado_of_1091 "London tornado of 1091").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-101)

### Earliest-known tornado in the Americas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Earliest-known tornado in the Americas")]

*   An apparent tornado is recorded to have struck [Tlatelolco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tlatelolco_(altepetl) "Tlatelolco (altepetl)") (present day [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City")), on August 21, 1521, two days before the Aztec capital's fall to [Cortés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hern%C3%A1n_Cort%C3%A9s "Hernán Cortés"). Many other tornadoes are documented historically within the [Basin of Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basin_of_Mexico "Basin of Mexico").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-102)

#### First confirmed tornado and first tornado fatality in present-day United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: First confirmed tornado and first tornado fatality in present-day United States")]

*   August 1671 – [Rehoboth, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rehoboth,_Massachusetts "Rehoboth, Massachusetts")[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Grazulis2001a-52)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-usatoday-103)
*   July 8, 1680 – [Cambridge, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge,_Massachusetts "Cambridge, Massachusetts") – 1 death[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Significant_Tornadoes-17)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-tornadochaser-104)

### Earliest-known tornado in Asia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Earliest-known tornado in Asia")]

*   A tornado was observed in [Kaifeng Prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaifeng_Prefecture "Kaifeng Prefecture") during the summer of AD 967.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-105)
*   An apparent tornado caused severe damage in [Heian-kyō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heian-ky%C5%8D "Heian-kyō") in modern-day [Kyoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kyoto "Kyoto") on 1 June 1180,[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-106) which was recorded by Japanese author [Kamo no Chōmei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamo_no_Ch%C5%8Dmei "Kamo no Chōmei"), who personally experienced the tornado.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-107)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-108)
*   The earliest recorded tornado in continental Asia struck near the city of [Calcutta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calcutta "Calcutta") in present-day [West Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal "West Bengal"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), in 1838. It was described as moving remarkably slow across its 16-mile (26 km) path southeast over the span of 2 to 3 hours. It was recorded to cause significant damage to the area, including 3.5-pound (1.6 kg) hail being observed at the [Dum Dum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dum_Dum "Dum Dum") weather observatory.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-109)

### First published scientific studies of a tornado

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: First published scientific studies of a tornado")]

A few scientists in Europe,[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-110) the US, and elsewhere documented the occurrence of tornadoes in the late 18th and early-mid 19th centuries to try to discern [patterns of distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_climatology "Tornado climatology") and sometimes with inferences about [formative processes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadogenesis "Tornadogenesis") and dynamics.

For intensive studies of tornadoes, these are the earliest known [publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_journal "Scientific journal"):

*   1765: German scientist [Gottlob Burchard Genzmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottlob_Burchard_Genzmer "Gottlob Burchard Genzmer") published a detailed survey of the damage path of an extremely violent tornado which occurred near [Woldegk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woldegk "Woldegk"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), on 29 June 1764. It covers the entire 33 km (18.6 mi) long track and also includes eyewitness reports as well as an analysis of the debris and hail fallout areas. Genzmer calls the event an "Orcan" and only compares it to [waterspouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterspout "Waterspout") or [dust devils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust_devil "Dust devil"). Based on the damage survey, modern day meteorologists from the [ESSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Severe_Storms_Laboratory "European Severe Storms Laboratory") gave an roughly estimated rating of F5.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-111)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-112)
*   1839–41: A detailed survey of the damage path of [the significant tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1835_New_Brunswick,_New_Jersey_tornado "1835 New Brunswick, New Jersey tornado") that struck [New Brunswick, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Brunswick,_New_Jersey "New Brunswick, New Jersey"), on 19 June 1835, was published. This tornado is also considered the deadliest tornado in New Jersey history. The path was surveyed by many scientists on account of its location between New York City and Philadelphia, including early tornado theorists [James Pollard Espy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Pollard_Espy "James Pollard Espy") and [William Charles Redfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Charles_Redfield "William Charles Redfield"). Scientists disagreed whether there was whirling, convergent, or rotational motion. A conclusion that remains accurate today is that the most intense [damage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_intensity "Tornado intensity") tends to be on the right side of a tornado (with respect to direction of forward movement), which was found to be generally easterly.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-113)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-114)
*   1840: The earliest known intensive study of a tornadic event published in Europe, by French scientist Athanase Peltier.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-115)
*   1865: The first in India and earliest known scientific survey of a tornado that analyzed structure and dynamics was published in 1865 by Indian scientist Chunder Sikur Chatterjee. The path damage survey of a tornado that occurred at Pundooah (now [Pandua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandua,_Hooghly "Pandua, Hooghly")), [Hugli district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hooghly_district "Hooghly district"), [West Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal "West Bengal"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), was documented on maps and revealed [multiple vortices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_vortex_tornado "Multiple vortex tornado"), the [tornadocyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadocyclone "Tornadocyclone"), and direction of rotation,[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-116) predating work by [John Park Finley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Park_Finley "John Park Finley"), [Alfred Wegener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Wegener "Alfred Wegener"), [Johannes Letzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Letzmann "Johannes Letzmann"), and [Ted Fujita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Fujita "Ted Fujita").

### Years without tornado rated violent (F4/EF4+) in United States

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Years without tornado rated violent (F4/EF4+) in United States")]

2018 was the only year since official records began in 1950 that no tornado in the United States was rated in the violent class (F4/EF4+).[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-119) Worldwide, however, there were two violent tornadoes- one in Brazil[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-120) and one in Canada.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-121)

## Exceptional survivors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Exceptional survivors")]

### Longest distance carried by a tornado

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Longest distance carried by a tornado")]

Matt Suter of [Fordland, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fordland,_Missouri "Fordland, Missouri") holds the record for the longest-known distance traveled by anyone picked up by a tornado who survived the ordeal. On March 12, 2006, he was carried 1,307 feet (398 m), 13 feet (4.0 m) shy of one quarter-mile (402 m), according to National Weather Service measurements.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-122)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-123)

While not officially reported as the longest distance, both the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") and tornado expert [Thomas P. Grazulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis "Thomas P. Grazulis") document that the [1976 Brownwood, Texas, F5 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Brownwood_tornado "1976 Brownwood tornado") picked up and threw two teenagers 1,000 yards (910 m), with both surviving.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-124)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-125)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-126)

### Arabi, Louisiana

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=35 "Edit section: Arabi, Louisiana")]

On March 22, 2022, [an EF3 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_March_21%E2%80%9323,_2022#Gretna%E2%80%93Arabi%E2%80%93New_Orleans_East,_Louisiana "Tornado outbreak of March 21–23, 2022") struck [Arabi, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabi,_Louisiana "Arabi, Louisiana"), a [census-designated place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Census-designated_place "Census-designated place") in the [New Orleans metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_metropolitan_area "New Orleans metropolitan area"). On December 14 of that year, [another tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_December_12%E2%80%9315,_2022#December_14_event "Tornado outbreak of December 12–15, 2022"), rated EF2, affected many of the same areas, with the two tornado tracks overlapping in parts of [Terrytown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrytown,_Louisiana "Terrytown, Louisiana") and [Arabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabi,_Louisiana "Arabi, Louisiana").[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-127)

### Barnsley, Kentucky

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=36 "Edit section: Barnsley, Kentucky")]

The unincorporated community of [Barnsley, Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnsley,_Kentucky "Barnsley, Kentucky") was hit twice by intense tornadoes less than three years apart from each other.

The violent [2021 Western Kentucky tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado "2021 Western Kentucky tornado") hit the community, destroying numerous homes, and in 2024, the city was struck again by an [EF3 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_May_25%E2%80%9327,_2024#Eddyville%E2%80%93Crider%E2%80%93Charleston%E2%80%93Barnsley,_Kentucky "Tornado outbreak of May 25–27, 2024") that impacted many of the same areas. Certain areas in Barnsley were affected by both tornadoes.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-128)

### Chaffee, Kelso and Illmo, Missouri

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=37 "Edit section: Chaffee, Kelso and Illmo, Missouri")]

On April 30, 1940, two separate tornadoes, less than two hours apart, struck the communities of [Chaffee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaffee,_Missouri "Chaffee, Missouri"), [Kelso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelso,_Missouri "Kelso, Missouri") and [Illmo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illmo,_Scott_City,_Missouri "Illmo, Scott City, Missouri"), [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Significant_Tornadoes-17)[Thomas P. Grazulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis "Thomas P. Grazulis") rated both tornadoes F2 on the Fujita scale and both tornadoes killed one person near Kelso.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Significant_Tornadoes-17)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

List of world records related to tornadoes

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Super_Outbreak_Map.jpg/250px-Super_Outbreak_Map.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Super_Outbreak_Map.jpg)

A map of the tornado paths in the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak")

This article lists various **tornado records**. The most "extreme" [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado "Tornado") in recorded history was the [Tri-State tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1925_Tri-State_tornado "1925 Tri-State tornado"), which spread through parts of [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri"), [Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illinois "Illinois"), and [Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana "Indiana") on March 18, 1925. It was likely an F5 on the [Fujita Scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_Scale "Fujita Scale") (tornadoes were not rated at the time) and holds records for longest path length at 219 miles (352 km) and longest duration at about 3+1⁄2 hours. The 2014 [Pilger, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilger,_Nebraska "Pilger, Nebraska") tornado had the highest forward speed ever recorded in a violent tornado, at 94 mph (151 km/h). The deadliest tornado in world history was the [Daulatpur–Saturia tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daulatpur%E2%80%93Saturia_tornado "Daulatpur–Saturia tornado") in Bangladesh on April 26, 1989, which killed approximately 1,300 people.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Bangladesh_tornado-1) In the history of Bangladesh, at least 24 tornadoes killed more than 100 people each, almost half of the total for the world.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-2) The most extensive [tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak "Tornado outbreak") on record was the [2011 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Super_Outbreak "2011 Super Outbreak"), which resulted in 367 tornadoes and 324 tornadic fatalities,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-super_outbreak-3) whereas the [1974 Super Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Super_Outbreak "1974 Super Outbreak") was the [most intense tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tornado_outbreaks_by_outbreak_intensity_score "List of tornado outbreaks by outbreak intensity score") on tornado expert [Thomas P. Grazulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis "Thomas P. Grazulis")'s [outbreak intensity score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis#Outbreak_intensity_score "Thomas P. Grazulis") with 578, as opposed to the 2011 outbreak's 378.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-4) The widest tornado recorded was the [2013 El Reno tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_El_Reno_tornado "2013 El Reno tornado"), having a width of 2.6 miles (4.2 km), and killing eight people including veteran storm chaser [Tim Samaras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Samaras "Tim Samaras").

The 2011 Super Outbreak was the largest tornado outbreak spawned by a single weather system in recorded history; it produced 367 tornadoes from April 25–28, with 223 of those in a single 24-hour period on April 27 from midnight to midnight [CDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Time_Zone "Central Time Zone"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-2011NCDC-5)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-tornado-largest-tornado-outbreak-12) fifteen of which were violent EF4–EF5 tornadoes. 348 deaths occurred in that outbreak, of which 324 were tornado-related. The outbreak largely contributed to the record for most tornadoes in April with [780 tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_tornadoes_in_April_2011 "List of United States tornadoes in April 2011"), almost triple the prior record (267 in April 1974). The overall record for a single month was 542 in May 2003, which was also broken.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-April_2011_tornado_information-13)

The 1974 Super Outbreak of April 3–4, which spawned 148 confirmed tornadoes across eastern North America, held the record for the most prolific tornado outbreak in terms of overall tornadoes for many years, and as of October 2025, it still holds the record for most violent, long-track tornadoes (7 F5 and 23 F4 tornadoes). More significant tornadoes occurred within 24 hours than any other day on record.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-1974NCDC-6)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-tornado_outbreak_sequences-14) Due to advancements in technology allowing for more accuracy in tornado reporting, the 2011 and 1974 tornado counts are not directly comparable.

### Longest continuous outbreak and largest autumnal outbreak

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Longest continuous outbreak and largest autumnal outbreak")]

Most tornado outbreaks in North America occur in the spring, but there is a secondary peak of tornado activity in the fall. It is historically less consistent from year to year but can include exceptionally large or intense outbreaks. In 1992, an estimated [95 tornadoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_1992_tornado_outbreak "November 1992 tornado outbreak") broke out in a record 41 hours of continuous [tornado activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/November_1992_tornado_outbreak "November 1992 tornado outbreak") from November 21 to 23. This is also among the largest-known outbreaks in areal expanse. Many other very large outbreaks have occurred in autumn, especially in October and November, such as the [2002 Veterans Day weekend](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_November_9%E2%80%9311,_2002 "Tornado outbreak of November 9–11, 2002") outbreak, in which 83 tornadoes occurred from November 9 to 11, and [November 17, 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_November_17,_2013 "Tornado outbreak of November 17, 2013"), when 73 tornadoes were produced in 11 hours.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Significant_Tornadoes-17)

### Greatest number of tornadoes spawned from a hurricane

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Greatest number of tornadoes spawned from a hurricane")]

The greatest number of tornadoes spawned from a hurricane is 120 from [Hurricane Ivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Ivan_tornado_outbreak "Hurricane Ivan tornado outbreak") in September 2004, followed by [Hurricane Beulah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Beulah "Hurricane Beulah") with 115 in September 1967, and 103 from [Hurricane Frances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Frances_tornado_outbreak "Hurricane Frances tornado outbreak") in September 2004 (a couple weeks before Ivan).[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-18) Hurricanes prior to the 1990s, when tornado records were more sparse, perhaps produced more tornadoes than were officially documented.

### Most tornadoes in a single year

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Most tornadoes in a single year")]

On average, 1,200 tornadoes happen in a year in the United States. The most confirmed tornadoes in a single year was in [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadoes_of_2004 "Tornadoes of 2004"),[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-26) which had 1817 confirmed tornadoes. This was mostly boosted by a large tornado outbreak sequence in May 2004, where 509 tornadoes occurred. It also had help from a very active fall and winter tornado season.

## Tornado casualties and damage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Tornado casualties and damage")]

### Deadliest single tornado in world history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Deadliest single tornado in world history")]

Officially, the deadliest single tornado occurred on April 26, 1989, in Bangladesh, where a [large tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daulatpur%E2%80%93Saturia_tornado "Daulatpur–Saturia tornado") took at least 1,300 lives.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-27) In 2022, this tornado's death toll was challenged in a database of Bangladeshi tornadoes maintained by Dr. Fahim Sufi with the [Australian Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Government "Australian Government"), claiming that the April 14, 1969, [Dhaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhaka "Dhaka") tornado, which killed 922 people, was the deadliest in Bangladesh, with the Jamalpur tornado killing only 570.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-2023_Sustainability-28)

### Deadliest single tornado in US history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Deadliest single tornado in US history")]

The [Tri-State tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1925_Tri-State_tornado "1925 Tri-State tornado") of March 18, 1925, killed 695 people in Missouri (11), Illinois (613), and Indiana (71). The outbreak it occurred with was also the deadliest known tornado outbreak, with a combined death toll of 747 across the [Mississippi River Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi_River_Valley "Mississippi River Valley").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-NOAA/NWS_1925_Tri-State_Tornado_Statistics-29)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Tri-State_Tornado_Facts-30)

### Most intense tornado damage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Most intense tornado damage")]

The original [Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale "Fujita scale"), developed by [Ted Fujita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Fujita "Ted Fujita"), has never been used to assign a final rating over F5 intensity;[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-32) however, two tornadoes, the [1970 Lubbock tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Lubbock_tornado "1970 Lubbock tornado") and [1974 Xenia tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Xenia_tornado "1974 Xenia tornado"), were initially given F6 ratings by Fujita himself, but both were eventually downgraded to F5 ratings.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-33)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-34) The [1976 Jordan tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Jordan_tornado "1976 Jordan tornado") was described by Fujita as the most intense tornado damage he had surveyed up to that point.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-35)

A more recent example of extreme damage was at the Double Creek Estates of [Jarrell, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jarrell,_Texas "Jarrell, Texas"); the [1997 Jarrell tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_Jarrell_tornado "1997 Jarrell tornado") stalled over the area at peak F5 intensity, destroying every home in the subdivision, and killing 27. Extreme ground scouring and high-end F5 damage was surveyed.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-36) The [2008 Parkersburg tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Parkersburg_tornado "2008 Parkersburg tornado") was reported by mayor Bob Haylock to have been so intense that a majority of the fatalities out of [Parkersburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parkersburg,_Iowa "Parkersburg, Iowa") were from people taking shelter in basements underground.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-37) The [2011 Philadelphia, Mississippi tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Philadelphia,_Mississippi_tornado "2011 Philadelphia, Mississippi tornado") caused extreme ground scouring across its path; up to .5 m (1.6 ft) of soil was removed from the environment, presumably from intense [subvortices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-vortex_tornado "Multi-vortex tornado").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-BAMS-38)

### Most damaging tornado

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Most damaging tornado")]

The [1896 St. Louis–East St. Louis tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896_St._Louis%E2%80%93East_St._Louis_tornado "1896 St. Louis–East St. Louis tornado") on May 27, incurred the most damages adjusted for inflation, with an estimated $5.36 billion (2022 USD). In raw numbers, the [Joplin tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Joplin_tornado "2011 Joplin tornado") of May 22, 2011, is considered the costliest tornado in recent history, with damage totals at $3.71 billion (2022 USD). Until April 2011, the [Bridge Creek–Moore tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Bridge_Creek-Moore_tornado "1999 Bridge Creek-Moore tornado") of May 3, 1999, was the most costly, which was later surpassed by the [2011 Tuscaloosa–Birmingham tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Tuscaloosa%E2%80%93Birmingham_tornado "2011 Tuscaloosa–Birmingham tornado"), with a damage total of $3.18 billion (2022 USD).[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-tornado_damage_normalization-39)

During the F5 [1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Bridge_Creek%E2%80%93Moore_tornado "1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado") on May 3, 1999, in the southern [Oklahoma City metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_Metropolitan_Area "Oklahoma City Metropolitan Area") area, a [Doppler on Wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doppler_on_Wheels "Doppler on Wheels") situated near the tornado measured winds of 301±20 mph (484±32 km/h) momentarily in a small area inside the funnel approximately 100 m (330 ft) above ground level.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-57) The measured winds in this tornado have been updated to 321 miles per hour (517 km/h).[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Dow2024-40)

On May 31, 2013, a tornado hit rural areas near [El Reno, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Reno,_Oklahoma "El Reno, Oklahoma"). The tornado was originally rated as an EF3 based on damage; however, after mobile radar data analysis was conducted, it was concluded to have been an EF5 due to a measured wind speed of greater than 296 mph (476 km/h), second only to the Bridge Creek–Moore tornado. Revised RaXPol analysis found winds of 302±34 mph (486±55 km/h) well above ground level and ≥291 mph (468 km/h) below 10 m (33 ft) with some subvortices moving at 175 mph (282 km/h).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-RaXPol-58) These winds may possibly be as high or higher than the winds recorded on May 3, 1999. Despite the recorded windspeed, the El Reno tornado was later downgraded back to EF3 due to the fact that no EF5 damage was found, likely due to the lack of sufficient damage indicators in the largely-rural area west of [Oklahoma City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City "Oklahoma City").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-59)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-60)

During the [Greenfield, Iowa EF4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Greenfield_tornado "2024 Greenfield tornado") on May 21, 2024, [Doppler on Wheels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doppler_on_Wheels "Doppler on Wheels") recorded wind speeds of 263–271 mph (423–436 km/h) in a very small swath inside the funnel approximately 100–106 ft (30–32 m) above radar level as the tornado went through town. After doing some mathematical and physics-based calculations, the researchers determined those measured winds were equivalent to 309–318 mph (497–512 km/h). The calculated minimum wind threshold as stated beats both the [1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Bridge_Creek%E2%80%93Moore_tornado "1999 Bridge Creek–Moore tornado") and the [2013 El Reno, Oklahoma tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_El_Reno_tornado "2013 El Reno tornado") for minimum possible maximum windspeed; however, the highest confirmed peak windspeeds are lower than the 1999 tornado.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Wurman-2024-61)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-:3-62)

Winds were measured at 262–280 mph (422–451 km/h) using portable [Doppler weather radar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weather_radar#Velocity "Weather radar") in the [Red Rock, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Rock,_Oklahoma "Red Rock, Oklahoma"), tornado during the [April 26, 1991, tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/April_26,_1991_tornado_outbreak "April 26, 1991 tornado outbreak") in north-central Oklahoma. Though these winds are possibly indicative of F5 intensity, this particular tornado's path never encountered any significant structures and caused minimal damage, so it was rated F4.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Doppler_Spectra-51)

### Longest damage path and duration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Longest damage path and duration")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Radar_collage_of_a_long-lived_supercell_radar_on_December_10-11%2C_2021.png/250px-Radar_collage_of_a_long-lived_supercell_radar_on_December_10-11%2C_2021.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Radar_collage_of_a_long-lived_supercell_radar_on_December_10-11,_2021.png)

Radar collage of the [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") that spawned the record-breaking [tornado family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_family "Tornado family") on December 10–11, 2021

The longest-known track for a single tornado is the [Tri-State tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1925_Tri-State_tornado "1925 Tri-State tornado"), occurring on March 18, 1925, with a path length of 151 to 235 mi (243 to 378 km). For years there was debate whether the originally-recognized path length of 219 mi (352 km) over 3.5 hours was from one tornado or a series. Some very long track (VLT) tornadoes were later determined to be successive tornadoes spawned by the same supercell thunderstorm, which are known as a [tornado family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_family "Tornado family"). The Tri-State tornado, however, appeared to have no gaps in the damage. A six-year reanalysis study by a team of severe convective storm meteorologists found insufficient evidence to make firm conclusions but does conclude that it is likely that the beginning and ending of the path was resultant of separate tornadoes comprising a tornado family. It also found that the tornado began 15 mi (24 km) to the west and ended 1 mi (1.6 km) farther east than previously known, bringing the total path to 235 mi (378 km).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The 174 mi (280 km) segment from central [Madison County, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madison_County,_Missouri "Madison County, Missouri"), to [Pike County, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pike_County,_Indiana "Pike County, Indiana"), is likely one continuous tornado, and the 151 mi (243 km) segment from central [Bollinger County, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bollinger_County,_Missouri "Bollinger County, Missouri"), to western Pike County, Indiana, is very likely a single continuous tornado. Another [significant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_tornado_terms#S "Glossary of tornado terms") tornado was found about 65 mi (105 km) east-northeast of the end of aforementioned segment(s) of the Tri-State tornado family and is likely another member of the family. Its path length of 20 mi (32 km) over about 20 minutes makes the known tornado family path length total to 320 mi (510 km) over about 5+1⁄2 hours.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Johns-73)[Grazulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis "Thomas P. Grazulis") in 2001 wrote that the first 60 mi (97 km) of the (originally recognized) track is probably the result of two or more tornadoes and that a path length of 157 mi (253 km) was seemingly continuous.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Grazulis2001a-52)

The [2021 Western Kentucky tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado "2021 Western Kentucky tornado") on December 10, 2021, is the longest confirmed track of a tornado.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-74) This violent tornado tracked 165.7 mi (266.7 km) through the states of [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee") and [Kentucky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky "Kentucky") during a [very intense late-season outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_December_10%E2%80%9311,_2021 "Tornado outbreak of December 10–11, 2021"). The tornado was spawned by a very long-tracked [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") that previously dropped [another violent tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Tri-State_tornado "2021 Tri-State tornado") in [Arkansas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arkansas "Arkansas"), [Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Missouri "Missouri") and [Tennessee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee "Tennessee"), and initial media reports referred to the entire event as the "Quad-state Tornado", which would have had a path of 230 mi (370 km).[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-75)

On March 22, 1953, a tornado touched down near [Leesville, Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leesville,_Louisiana "Leesville, Louisiana") at 21:00 [UTC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UTC "UTC"); the tornado continued into far-northwest [Mississippi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mississippi "Mississippi"), before dissipating north of [Leland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leland,_Mississippi "Leland, Mississippi"), killing two and injuring 22. The tornado was rated F2 on the [Fujita scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fujita_scale "Fujita scale"). It traveled for 234.7 mi (377.7 km), making it possibly the longest tracked tornado in history, though it is likely that the path consisted of multiple different tornadoes as part of a [tornado family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_family "Tornado family").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-76)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-77)

### Longest path and duration tornado family

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Longest path and duration tornado family")]

What at one time was thought to be the record holder for the longest tornado path is now thought to be the longest tornado family, with a track of at least 293 miles (472 km) on May 26, 1917, from the Missouri border across Illinois into Indiana. It caused severe damage and mass casualties in [Charleston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charleston,_Illinois "Charleston, Illinois") and [Mattoon, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattoon,_Illinois "Mattoon, Illinois").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Significant_Tornadoes-17)

What was probably the longest track [supercell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supercell "Supercell") thunderstorm tracked 790 miles (1,270 km) across 6 states in 17.5 hours on March 12, 2006, as part of the [March 2006 tornado outbreak sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/March_2006_tornado_outbreak_sequence "March 2006 tornado outbreak sequence"). It began in [Noble County, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noble_County,_Oklahoma "Noble County, Oklahoma"), and ended in [Jackson County, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_County,_Michigan "Jackson County, Michigan"), producing many tornadoes in Missouri and Illinois.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-six_state_supercell-78)

### Largest path width

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Largest path width")]

Main article: [List of tornadoes by width](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tornadoes_by_width "List of tornadoes by width")

Officially, the widest tornado on record is the [El Reno, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Reno,_Oklahoma "El Reno, Oklahoma")[tornado of May 31, 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_El_Reno_tornado "2013 El Reno tornado"), with a width of 2.6 miles (4.2 km) at its peak. This is the width found by the National Weather Service based on preliminary data from University of Oklahoma RaXPol mobile radar that also sampled winds of 296 mph (476 km/h), which was used to upgrade the tornado to EF5.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-79) However, it was revealed that these winds did not impact any structures, and as a result the tornado was downgraded to EF3 based on damage.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-80)

The F4 [Hallam, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallam,_Nebraska "Hallam, Nebraska"), [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Hallam_tornado "2004 Hallam tornado") during the [outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_2004_tornado_outbreak_sequence "May 2004 tornado outbreak sequence") of May 22, 2004, was the previous official record holder for the widest tornado, surveyed at 2.5 miles (4.0 km) wide. A similar size tornado struck [Edmonson, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonson,_Texas "Edmonson, Texas") on May 31, 1968, when a damage path width between 2 and 3 miles (3.2 and 4.8 km) was recorded from an F3 tornado.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-81) Another tornado with a similar width struck [Maxton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxton,_North_Carolina "Maxton, North Carolina") and [Red Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Springs,_North_Carolina "Red Springs, North Carolina") during the [March 28, 1984, Carolina Tornado Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Carolinas_tornado_outbreak "1984 Carolinas tornado outbreak"); this tornado had a width of 2.5 miles wide at one point. Rated as F4, the tornado resulted in 3 fatalities and 280 injuries.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-82) The EF4 [Jiangsu tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jiangsu_tornado "Jiangsu tornado") on June 23, 2016, also had a peak width of 4.1 km wide (2.55 miles).[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-83)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-twister.caps.ou.edu-84)

On May 3, 1999, a Doppler On Wheels (DOW) mobile radar observed an F4 tornado as it crossed Mulhall during the [1999 Oklahoma Tornado Outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Oklahoma_Tornado_Outbreak "1999 Oklahoma Tornado Outbreak"), which also produced the [Bridge Creek–Moore tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Bridge_Creek-Moore_tornado "1999 Bridge Creek-Moore tornado"). The DOW documented the largest-ever-observed core flow circulation with a distance of 1,600 m (5,200 ft) between peak velocities on either side of the tornado, and a roughly 7 km (4.3 mi) width of peak wind gusts exceeding 43 m/s (96 mph), making the Mulhall tornado the largest tornado ever measured quantitatively.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-FARM-44)

On April 21, 1946, a [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_United_States_tornadoes_in_1946#April_21_event "List of United States tornadoes in 1946") struck the area in and around [Timber Lake, South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timber_Lake,_South_Dakota "Timber Lake, South Dakota"). The [U.S. Weather Bureau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") published a paper in 1946 stating the width of this tornado was 4 miles (6.4 km), which would make this the widest tornado ever documented in history. However, this is outside the period of reliable documentation accepted by the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service"), which is 1950–present.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-April_MWR-85)

On [May 19, 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_May_19%E2%80%9322,_2024 "Tornado outbreak of May 19–22, 2024"), a large [multiple-vortex tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple-vortex_tornado "Multiple-vortex tornado") tracked 15 mi (24 km) over rural areas near [Custer City, Oklahoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Custer_City,_Oklahoma "Custer City, Oklahoma"). While the tornado is believed to only have been about 1 mile wide, the maximum width of its tornadic windfield and accompanying damage was nearly 3 mi (4.8 km), making it one of the largest recorded damage paths of any tornado.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-86)

### Smallest and shortest-lived damaging tornado

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Smallest and shortest-lived damaging tornado")]

The smallest and shortest-lived tornado on record to produce surveyable damage was an EF1 tornado on the western side of [Broken Bow, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broken_Bow,_Nebraska "Broken Bow, Nebraska") on July 16, 2024. Spawned from an [outflow-driven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outflow_(meteorology) "Outflow (meteorology)") supercell, a very brief tornado, seen by a chaser and a [surveillance camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surveillance_camera "Surveillance camera"), was recorded on the ground for only two seconds, having a listed maximum width of only 1 yard (0.91 m) and a listed path length of 0.01 miles (16 m). Despite this, it was powerful enough to lift and throw a 800 lb (360 kg) trailer into a nearby parked car.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-87)

### Highest forward speed

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Highest forward speed")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Pilger%2C_NE_tornadoes.jpg/250px-Pilger%2C_NE_tornadoes.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pilger,_NE_tornadoes.jpg)

Twin EF4 tornadoes in [Pilger, Nebraska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilger,_Nebraska "Pilger, Nebraska") on June 16, 2014. The leftmost tornado would achieve the highest forward speed in history.

The highest accepted forward [speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speed "Speed") of an intense tornado on record was 75 mph (121 km/h) from the [1974 Guin tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Guin_tornado "1974 Guin tornado") that tore across northwestern Alabama. Other weak tornadoes have approached or exceeded this speed, but this is the fastest forward movement observed in a major tornado.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Significant_Tornadoes-17) The [1977 Birmingham tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_outbreak_of_April_1977#Birmingham%E2%80%93Smithfield,_Alabama "Tornado outbreak of April 1977") had an average forward speed of 60 mph (97 km/h),[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-88) as did the [2021 Western Kentucky tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Western_Kentucky_tornado "2021 Western Kentucky tornado").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-89)

Weaker tornadoes and tornado vortices have been recorded exceeding these speeds. Subvortices of the [2013 El Reno tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_El_Reno_tornado "2013 El Reno tornado") were recorded to travel at speeds of 175 mph (282 km/h) as they orbited the main vortex; the fastest speed a separate tornado-producing mesocyclone has been recorded to travel at was determined via [photogrammetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photogrammetry "Photogrammetry") to be the junior EF4 of the [2014 Pilger, Nebraska, tornado family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Pilger,_Nebraska,_tornado_family "2014 Pilger, Nebraska, tornado family"), travelling at 94.6 mph (152.2 km/h) for five seconds near the very end of its lifespan.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-90) These figures have not been acknowledged by the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service").

Calculations of highest speeds from the [National Centers for Environmental Information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Centers_for_Environmental_Information "National Centers for Environmental Information") Storm Events Database gives a high [average forward speed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Average_speed "Average speed") of a significant tornado just west of [Galt, Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galt,_Iowa "Galt, Iowa"), on December 15, 2021, of between 70.91 mph (114.12 km/h) and 88.65 mph (142.67 km/h).[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-91) This tornado occurred during the [December 2021 Midwest derecho and tornado outbreak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/December_2021_Midwest_derecho_and_tornado_outbreak "December 2021 Midwest derecho and tornado outbreak"), and was accompanied by straight-line winds approaching 80 mph (130 km/h). A faster range can be calculated on an EF1 tornado south of [Taylorville, Illinois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taylorville,_Illinois "Taylorville, Illinois") on [March 31, 2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tornadoes_in_the_tornado_outbreak_of_March_31_%E2%80%93_April_1,_2023#Illinois_(March_31) "List of tornadoes in the tornado outbreak of March 31 – April 1, 2023"), which traveled 1.74 mi (2.80 km) between 18:13 and 18:14, giving a range of forward speeds between 52.2 mph (84.0 km/h) and 104.4 mph (168.0 km/h).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-92) Due to significant variability caused by the unspecific nature of the timestamps provided, these speed figures are unofficial.

### Greatest pressure drop

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Greatest pressure drop")]

A [pressure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmospheric_pressure "Atmospheric pressure") deficit of 100 millibars (2.95 inHg) was observed during a violent [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Manchester_tornado "2003 Manchester tornado") near [Manchester, South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester,_South_Dakota "Manchester, South Dakota") on June 24, 2003, passed directly over an [in-situ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In-situ "In-situ") probe deployed by storm chasing researcher [Tim Samaras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Samaras "Tim Samaras").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Manchester-93) In less than a minute, the pressure plunged to 850 millibars (25.10 inHg) at ground level, widely regarded as the lowest reliably measured pressure inside a tornado and, when adjusted to sea level, comparable to the lowest pressures ever recorded in the United States.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-94)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Cerveny-95)

On April 21, 2007, a 194-millibar (5.73 inHg) pressure deficit was reported when a [tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_late-April_2007_tornado_outbreak_sequence_tornadoes "List of late-April 2007 tornado outbreak sequence tornadoes") struck a [storm chasing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storm_chasing "Storm chasing") vehicle in [Tulia, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulia,_Texas "Tulia, Texas").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-Tulia-96) The tornado caused EF2 damage as it passed through Tulia. The reported pressure drop far exceeds that which would be expected based on theoretical calculations.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-JAS3489-97)

There is a questionable and unofficial citizen's barometer measurement of a 192-millibar (5.67 inHg) drop around [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") in 1904.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-in-situ_history-98)

## Early tornadoes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Early tornadoes")]

### Earliest-known tornado in Europe

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Earliest-known tornado in Europe")]

*   The earliest recorded tornado in Europe struck [Freising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freising "Freising") (Germany) in 788.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-99)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-100)
*   The earliest-known Irish tornado appeared on April 30, 1054, in Rostella, near [Kilbeggan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilbeggan "Kilbeggan"). The earliest-known British tornado hit central London on October 23, 1091, and was [especially destructive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_tornado_of_1091 "London tornado of 1091").[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-101)

### Earliest-known tornado in the Americas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Earliest-known tornado in the Americas")]

### First published scientific studies of a tornado

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: First published scientific studies of a tornado")]

A few scientists in Europe,[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-110) the US, and elsewhere documented the occurrence of tornadoes in the late 18th and early-mid 19th centuries to try to discern [patterns of distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_climatology "Tornado climatology") and sometimes with inferences about [formative processes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadogenesis "Tornadogenesis") and dynamics.

For intensive studies of tornadoes, these are the earliest known [publications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_journal "Scientific journal"):

*   1765: German scientist [Gottlob Burchard Genzmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottlob_Burchard_Genzmer "Gottlob Burchard Genzmer") published a detailed survey of the damage path of an extremely violent tornado which occurred near [Woldegk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woldegk "Woldegk"), [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany"), on 29 June 1764. It covers the entire 33 km (18.6 mi) long track and also includes eyewitness reports as well as an analysis of the debris and hail fallout areas. Genzmer calls the event an "Orcan" and only compares it to [waterspouts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterspout "Waterspout") or [dust devils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dust_devil "Dust devil"). Based on the damage survey, modern day meteorologists from the [ESSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Severe_Storms_Laboratory "European Severe Storms Laboratory") gave an roughly estimated rating of F5.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-111)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-112)
*   1839–41: A detailed survey of the damage path of [the significant tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1835_New_Brunswick,_New_Jersey_tornado "1835 New Brunswick, New Jersey tornado") that struck [New Brunswick, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Brunswick,_New_Jersey "New Brunswick, New Jersey"), on 19 June 1835, was published. This tornado is also considered the deadliest tornado in New Jersey history. The path was surveyed by many scientists on account of its location between New York City and Philadelphia, including early tornado theorists [James Pollard Espy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Pollard_Espy "James Pollard Espy") and [William Charles Redfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Charles_Redfield "William Charles Redfield"). Scientists disagreed whether there was whirling, convergent, or rotational motion. A conclusion that remains accurate today is that the most intense [damage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_intensity "Tornado intensity") tends to be on the right side of a tornado (with respect to direction of forward movement), which was found to be generally easterly.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-113)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-114)
*   1840: The earliest known intensive study of a tornadic event published in Europe, by French scientist Athanase Peltier.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-115)
*   1865: The first in India and earliest known scientific survey of a tornado that analyzed structure and dynamics was published in 1865 by Indian scientist Chunder Sikur Chatterjee. The path damage survey of a tornado that occurred at Pundooah (now [Pandua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pandua,_Hooghly "Pandua, Hooghly")), [Hugli district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hooghly_district "Hooghly district"), [West Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Bengal "West Bengal"), [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"), was documented on maps and revealed [multiple vortices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_vortex_tornado "Multiple vortex tornado"), the [tornadocyclone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornadocyclone "Tornadocyclone"), and direction of rotation,[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-116) predating work by [John Park Finley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Park_Finley "John Park Finley"), [Alfred Wegener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Wegener "Alfred Wegener"), [Johannes Letzmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Letzmann "Johannes Letzmann"), and [Ted Fujita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Fujita "Ted Fujita").

### Longest distance carried by a tornado

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tornado_records&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Longest distance carried by a tornado")]

Matt Suter of [Fordland, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fordland,_Missouri "Fordland, Missouri") holds the record for the longest-known distance traveled by anyone picked up by a tornado who survived the ordeal. On March 12, 2006, he was carried 1,307 feet (398 m), 13 feet (4.0 m) shy of one quarter-mile (402 m), according to National Weather Service measurements.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-122)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-123)

While not officially reported as the longest distance, both the [National Weather Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Weather_Service "National Weather Service") and tornado expert [Thomas P. Grazulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_P._Grazulis "Thomas P. Grazulis") document that the [1976 Brownwood, Texas, F5 tornado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Brownwood_tornado "1976 Brownwood tornado") picked up and threw two teenagers 1,000 yards (910 m), with both surviving.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-124)[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-125)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tornado_records#cite_note-126)
